claim: On the authors' Bengali handwriting benchmark, a general multimodal LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash, prompted to transcribe exactly) had CER 19.39% / WER 32.49% on BN-HTRd (805 full-page images) and CER 37.42% / WER 56.39% on Bongabdo (111 images). The web OCR tool Imagetotext.info scored CER 20.90 / WER 37.10 on BN-HTRd but a better CER 14.36 / WER 31.14 on Bongabdo, so the ranking flips between datasets. Gemini 2.5 Pro is reported, without numbers, as slightly better than Flash; Flash was used because of free-tier API limits. Bengali only: Assamese and exam answer sheets were not tested.

The authors' purpose-built Bengali HTR model (decoder-only GPT-2 style, 87M parameters, grapheme tokenizer, trained from scratch) is their best configuration. It reaches CER 6.19% / WER 14.20% on BN-HTRd and CER 8.68% / WER 23.56% on Bongabdo, beating Gemini 2.5 Flash and Imagetotext.info on both sets. Even this best system gets roughly 1 in 7 to nearly 1 in 4 words wrong on clean white-background handwriting, so transcription errors would carry into any answer-grading step. The grapheme tokenizer cut model size from 162M (BPE) to 87M with lower error.
quote: outperforming both systems by a large margin

claim: Accuracy falls outside the training distribution and depends on word segmentation. In cross-dataset tests the proposed model reached CER 18.04% / WER 33.20% (trained on BanglaWriting, tested on BN-HTRd) and CER 12.66% / WER 24.79% (reverse). Excluding images where word detection failed improved BN-HTRd CER from 6.19 to 4.58 and WER from 14.20 to 12.59. The authors state the training data is mainly handwriting on white backgrounds, which is a concern for photographed exercise-book pages.
quote: limiting adaptability to more varied real-world scenarios

claim: A competitive Bengali HTR can be built and self-hosted cheaply. Training on one NVIDIA RTX 3080 took about 24 GPU-hours in total: 13 h on 4.5M synthetic line images, 9 h on 7M synthetic word images, and under 2 h fine-tuning on about 338,574 real word images. Inference ran at 9.95 words/s for the 87M model (8.30 words/s for the 162M variant). The Flask/Celery/Redis/Docker pipeline is released under the MIT licence, and its web UI shows the output in an editable text box for user correction, a basic human-in-the-loop design.
quote: we publicly release our complete pipeline under the MIT license

claim: The authors assert, without reporting numbers, that Gemini was chosen as the representative vision-language model because it substantially outperforms ChatGPT and Claude on Bengali handwriting. They also say other OCR services were excluded for lacking Bengali handwriting support, lacking APIs, or performing poorly in preliminary tests. This is a mid-2025 snapshot (Gemini 2.5 Flash) from a system-demonstration paper and may be outdated by Oct 2026. Treat it as a pointer for model selection, not as a measured comparison.
quote: substantially surpassing models such as ChatGPT and Claude on this task

claim: Henkel et al. (arXiv 2510.05538, Oct 2025) tested four then-frontier multimodal LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4.1) on 288 clean scanned worksheet answers from Ghanaian middle-school students (fractions, percentages, basic algebra; binary right/wrong judgement against double-checked human grades; human-to-human agreement near 100%). Only Gemini 2.5 Pro reached the headline 95% grading accuracy (linear weighted kappa 0.90); the others scored 77% (kappa 0.54, Claude 3.5), 79% (0.58, GPT-4.1) and 84% (0.68, Claude 3.7). Just reading the student's handwritten final answer (the 'vision' step) was right only 76-89% of the time (Claude 3.7 76%, Claude 3.5 79%, GPT-4.1 86%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 89%), even though the authors call the setting favorable. Scope is arithmetic only: no Indian-script, upper-secondary or multi-mark long-answer work was tested.
quote: achieving 89% vision accuracy and 95% grading accuracy

claim: Henkel et al. found that on 150 US elementary-school math drawings (DrawEDU subset, where the drawing is the answer), the same four models given only the image reached just 61-64% accuracy and kappa 0.15-0.38 against ground truth (abstract headline: 0.20). Adding a detailed human description of each drawing lifted kappa to 0.43-0.47 (72-75% accuracy), about the level of the two expert teachers' initial agreement (76% raw agreement, kappa 0.45). The authors judge a kappa of about 0.47 insufficient for real-world deployment, so diagram/figure answers are the weak point of photo-based AI grading; part of the gap is genuine ambiguity (10-20 of 150 items could legitimately be graded either way).
quote: they struggled, achieving only k = 0.20 with ground truth scores

claim: Henkel et al. report failure modes unlike human graders'. In the arithmetic test GPT-4.1 marked a worksheet wrong although the student's final answer was correct, because the intermediate working contained errors; the authors call rejecting correct answers over untidy or flawed working a non-human error pattern (their Figure 3 is captioned an MLLM grading hallucination). Error direction also varied by model: per the paper's text, wrongly accepting incorrect answers happened on 3.8% of responses for Gemini 2.5 Pro versus 14.2-20.8% for the two Claude models, while GPT-4.1 erred both ways (12.2% wrongly accepted, 9.0% wrongly rejected); Table 3's column headers are inconsistent with this text. Claude 3.7 and Gemini 2.5 Pro graded 8 and 6 points better than they read, which the authors take as models using maths context to cover misreads, a false-positive risk.
quote: rejecting correct final answers due to flawed intermediate steps

claim: Henkel et al. recommend hybrid human-in-the-loop deployment rather than autonomous grading: the model screens routine arithmetic and flags edge cases for educator review; for illustrations it should only pre-sort work by confidence so teachers focus where judgment is needed; systems should show teachers what the model attended to, not just the grade. They caution that their binary rubric and minimal prompting likely understate what careful prompt engineering could achieve, and that results are limited to the grade levels and maths domains studied.
quote: flagging edge cases for educator review

claim: A University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign study (Levine, Aenlle, Zilles, West, Silva; to be published at AIED 2026; arXiv v1, 18 May 2026) found that the best of three vision LLMs (Gemini-3-flash; the others were GPT-5-mini and GPT-5.1) agreed with instructor grading on 89-99% of rubric items per question, across five questions of photographed handwritten university maths. The headline figure is about 95%, an unweighted mean of the five question scores (my item-weighted recomputation from Table 1 gives about 94%). GPT-5-mini scored 89-98% and GPT-5.1 87-95%. The best model scored 96-99% on the three in-lecture extra-credit questions but only 89% and 93% on the two proctored-midterm questions; the paper does not explain the gap.
quote: Not a verbatim quote (quoting limited). Locator: Table 1 (rubric-item accuracy by question and model); Section 3 first paragraph; Section 4 Conclusion (95% figure); Section 2 Methods (course set-ups).

claim: Most disagreements with human graders came from the model misreading the photographed work, not from misapplying the marking rubric: 87% of the best model's errors were transcription errors. That 87% is an unweighted mean of five per-question shares ranging 71-100%; pooling by item counts from Table 1 gives roughly 75% (my own estimate). Documented causes were blurry, low-resolution, out-of-focus or motion-blurred photos (even with standardised document cameras), rotated text despite in-app rotation tools, and hallucinated text. Students could preview, crop and resubmit their images, which the authors say may contribute to the accuracy they observed. They conclude that better capture and preprocessing may yield larger gains than prompt tuning, and suggest pre-submission quality checks or a preview transcription.
quote: Not a verbatim quote (quoting limited). Locator: Abstract; Section 1 (paragraph on how this work differs from prior work); Section 3 opening paragraph and Section 3.1 (failure modes and fixes); Table 1 %TE and %RAE columns.

claim: The best model's errors skewed toward false positives (over-crediting) at about 2.5 to 1, sometimes hallucinating a correct answer that resembled the reference solution when handwriting was hard to read, most often on blurry or rotated images; the GPT models showed near parity between false positives and negatives. The only case where rubric-application errors exceeded transcription errors was GPT-5.1 on one question (12% false negatives), where it failed to accept a valid sign-reversed answer that the rubric allowed. The authors saw no consistent lenient-or-strict pattern by model or question, so they could not yet use model behaviour to auto-assign grades or flag submissions for manual review.
quote: Not a verbatim quote (quoting limited). Locator: Section 4 Conclusion (false-positive skew); Section 3.1 (hallucinated text); Section 3 (GPT-5.1 on C1-Q1 and the paragraph on lenient/strict patterns); Table 1 %FP and %FN columns.

claim: The authors judge the best model adequate only for low-stakes, formative use such as practice problems, and only if students are told the AI feedback may contain mistakes; they say high-stakes use needs greater reliability in interpreting student work. Their tool grades asynchronously after submissions close, lets human graders review and override AI results, and gives human grades precedence. This supports AI checking of practice answers but argues against presenting AI marks as board-equivalent scores.
quote: Levine et al. 2026, Section 4: "sufficient for low-stakes, formative contexts (e.g., practice problems)"

claim: Evidence gaps for ExamLeaf: the paper covers only English-language university maths from one large Midwestern US university, with no Indic-script, bilingual, school-level or board-marking-scheme material. It reports no per-submission cost or latency, only that the models' per-token costs are feasible for a production autograder. Ground truth came from instructors who are also the authors, with no inter-rater agreement reported, and Table 1's 600 submissions do not reconcile with the course sizes (440 and 245) given in Methods. Second-hand pointers from its literature review: a 2024 GPT-4V/MathPix/GPT-4 pipeline on scanned handwritten maths exams reached about 60% grading accuracy (arXiv:2408.11728), and a GPT-5 calculus-exam study (arXiv:2510.05162) reportedly needed manual review of 70% of items for a confidence-based human-in-the-loop grader to raise agreement. The paper prints R2 = 0.85 for both the unfiltered and human-in-the-loop graders, an apparent typo.
quote: Not a verbatim quote (quoting limited). Locator: Section 1 (prior-work paragraph citing Liu et al. and Kortemeyer et al.); Section 2 (courses, ground truth, models, cost remark); Table 1; no dedicated limitations section.

claim: In this Sept 2026 arXiv preprint (v2) on criterion-level grading of scanned handwritten undergraduate exam answers (485 answers, 1,982 criterion records; 291 held-out test criteria from 72 answers), Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct fine-tuned with LoRA on examiner-marked records reached QWK 0.727 and MAE 0.435 marks (60.8% exact match) against the course examiner. The mean QWK across the three human pairs (examiner plus two independent faculty markers) was 0.551, with pairwise MAE 0.687-0.746 marks. The two independent markers matched exactly on only 19.6% of criteria. The authors state the model-vs-human comparison reflects calibration to the examiner's training marks: the model learned from 1,483 examiner-assigned marks and the independent markers did not.
quote: "This comparison reflects calibration to the examiner’s training marks." (Tonmoy et al., arXiv:2609.14284v2, abstract)

claim: Prompting open VLMs without task-specific training was much weaker than adapting them. Zero-shot QWK was about 0.60 (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), 0.51 (InternVL3-8B) and 0.48 (Pixtral-12B). These are derived by subtracting the Table VII gains from the LoRA QWKs of 0.727, 0.707 and 0.659. Few-shot prompting (1 to 3 solved examples with images) lowered QWK by 0.005-0.051 in all four configurations with valid prompted scores. Zero-shot outputs often broke the required JSON format: strict parsing failed on 155/291 Qwen2.5-VL and 28/291 InternVL3 outputs, and marks had to be recovered by repair. The OCR-free Donut baseline produced no parsable marks when prompted and only about 52% coverage after adaptation (QWK 0.080 with LoRA, 0.295 with full fine-tuning, on the parsed subset only).
quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim (one-quote limit). Locator, arXiv:2609.14284v2: Table VII (change vs zero-shot), Section V.B (few-shot effect, Donut coverage), Section IV.B (JSON parse failures 155/291 and 28/291).

claim: Grading was not repeatable under sampling. Over five stochastic repetitions (temperature 0.7, decoding seed varied only) of the LoRA-adapted models on all 291 test criteria, ICC(2,1) was 0.790 (Qwen2.5-VL), 0.862 (Pixtral) and 0.874 (InternVL3). Yet 50.2-63.6% of criteria received different marks across the runs: exact repeatability was 49.8% InternVL3, 41.9% Qwen2.5-VL and 36.4% Pixtral, with mean per-item SD of 0.249-0.322 marks. The authors recommend greedy decoding for reported marks but say training and numerical reproducibility still need separate checks.
quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim (one-quote limit). Locator, arXiv:2609.14284v2: Section V.D (Study 3), Table X (ICC, per-item SD, share scored identically in all five runs), Fig. 6, abstract.

claim: Errors were concentrated by subject and by criterion weight. For Qwen2.5-VL with LoRA, subject-level MAE ranged from 0.125 marks (Fisheries) to 1.625 marks (Object-Oriented Programming, a code-bearing template with only 20 test judgments). MAE rose from 0.267 marks on criteria worth at most 2 marks (92 criteria) to 0.375 (2-3 marks, 76 criteria) and 0.598 (above 3 marks, 123 criteria). Per-template QWK ranged from 0.00 (Digital Image Processing) to 0.89 (Data Mining), based on only 8-45 judgments per template. The authors suggest prioritising such cases for teacher review.
quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim (one-quote limit). Locator, arXiv:2609.14284v2: Section V.E (Study 4), Table VIII and Table XI, Section V.G (RQ4 discussion).

claim: The evidence base is narrow relative to a phone-photo, school-board use case. Inputs were scanned multi-page answer PDFs rendered at 200 DPI, stitched into one image and fed to the models at a long side of 1,280 px (768 px for Pixtral); the extracted text mentions no smartphone photographs. Answers came from undergraduate final exams across nine subjects and 12 question templates, not Class 10/12 board papers. Training labels came from one examiner, the test split was 72 answers, and training used a single seed. No answer-language or script is stated in the extracted text, and no Indian-language or mixed-script handwriting test is reported. The study did not measure changes in teacher workload or student learning. The authors are Bangladesh-based and the work was funded by the Bangladesh Accreditation Council. The paper is internally inconsistent on provenance: Section IV.A says four institutions, Section V.H says one institution.
quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim (one-quote limit). Locator, arXiv:2609.14284v2: Section IV.A and Fig. 2 (scanned scripts, 200 DPI, four institutions), Section II.B and Table V (input resolution), Section V.H (one institution, one examiner, 72 test answers), Disclosure (funding).

claim: Ofqual, the regulator of GCSEs, AS/A levels and vocational qualifications in England, restates (citing its 2024 AI policy approach) that letting AI alone decide a student's mark in regulated high-stakes qualifications breaches its regulations. The paper still calls AI in marking, especially quality assurance, promising and says Ofqual supports exploring it. It is a discussion working paper that applies to England only. A text search of the page for India, CBSE, ASSEB, Assam, Bengali, Hindi and Devanagari returned no hits, so it gives no view on Indian boards or Indian-language scripts.
quote: [Paraphrase only; verbatim quote omitted under a one-short-quote limit. Locator: the sole-marker position is restated in the Executive summary, the Introduction and the Discussion section of the Ofqual working paper dated 14 Jan 2026.]

claim: The paper's overall evidence verdict is that current research does not establish that AI marking is valid for high-stakes qualifications in general. Only evidence specific to a given qualification, candidate population, construct and item type can support it, and that evidence is not yet widely available. It also notes that empirical studies find AI marking performance varies across demographic groups, so group-level fairness checks are needed.
quote: [Paraphrase only; verbatim quote omitted under a one-short-quote limit. Locator: Executive summary (Conclusions paragraph and the bias and fairness bullet) and the Discussion section.]

claim: Footnote 7, attached to the Section 3 text on handwritten scripts, warns that LLM-based handwriting transcription fails differently from older OCR. It can favour likely words over what the student literally wrote, silently correct perceived mistakes, reorder content, and give different outputs for the same input because of sampling. This matters for a photo-of-answers grader because the student's actual error is what must be marked. The paper sets handwriting recognition aside as out of scope and gives no error rates. Its marking discussion assumes answers are already in digital text, so the handwriting-to-text step is an unmeasured extra error source.
quote: Ofqual working paper (14 Jan 2026), footnote 7: "preferring common words over exact transcription, “correcting” perceived errors"

claim: The paper expects AI-generated marks to become acceptable sooner in formative and low-stakes assessment than in high-stakes use, which needs stronger safeguards and validity evidence. A self-practice answer checker that is not an official board exam would fall in the more permissive category. The paper states this as a forecast without a citation in that sentence, and it gives no Indian regulator's view.
quote: [Paraphrase only; verbatim quote omitted under a one-short-quote limit. Locator: Discussion section, paragraph on Ofqual's General Conditions for differentiating students, which ends with the formative and low-stakes forecast.]

claim: On human-in-the-loop design, the paper lists two models for an AI primary marker. One is a human second-marking all or a subset of responses. The other is experts only monitoring the statistical properties of auto-marked items. It calls the level of human involvement that suffices for accountability an open regulatory question. It also says current AI outputs are variable and unpredictable, with confidence measures that need not reflect real-world accuracy. Implication drawn by this extractor and not stated in the paper: routing only low-confidence answers to a human is weak, and random sampled audits are safer.
quote: [Paraphrase only; verbatim quote omitted under a one-short-quote limit. Locator: Executive summary, the accountability and oversight bullet and the summary of current AI characteristics.]

claim: Careers360 reports that the Ministry of Education has recommended that seven states (Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Kerala, Manipur, Odisha, Telangana and West Bengal) adopt a common board for both Class 10 and Class 12 exams, because together they accounted for 66% of student failures in 2024. Assam, West Bengal and Odisha, boards named in the ExamLeaf plan, are all on the list.
quote: "seven states adopt a common board"

claim: In the Ministry analysis of 2024 results (as reported by Careers360), the Uttar Pradesh Madhyamik Shiksha Parishad (UP Board) had the most students of all 66 boards: 27,49,364 in Class 10 and 24,52,830 in Class 12, with pass rates of 88.59% (Class 10) and 82.60% (Class 12). The article gives no examinee counts for Assam, West Bengal, Bihar or Odisha.
quote: [verbatim quote withheld to respect the one-short-quote limit; see the article paragraph naming the UP Board as the board with the most students]

claim: Ministry figures for the 2024 board exams (analysis published 18 June 2025): 1,85,53,676 students appeared at the secondary level (Class 10 by context), 25,264 more than in 2023, and 1,49,45,104 in Class 12 (down from 1,55,01,791 in 2023). Overall pass rate: Class 10 86.51% (84.93% in 2023); Class 12 88.50% in the article text (82.47% in 2023), but the article's own ten-year table shows 88.05% for Class 12 in 2024, so that figure needs checking against the primary Ministry release.
quote: [verbatim quote withheld to respect the one-short-quote limit; see the article's student-numbers paragraphs and its ten-year pass-percentage table]

claim: The Ministry analysis covers 66 school boards: 52 regular state boards, 2 central boards and 12 open-school boards (NIOS plus 11 state open boards). Eight boards were added from 2024, including the Delhi Board of School Education (DBSE), which the Delhi Government is dismantling. Several boards are tiny: in Class 10 the Bhartiya Shiksha Board, Haridwar had 96 students, DBSE 2,519 and the UP Sanskrit Board 19,232, against 27,49,364 for the UP Board.
quote: [verbatim quote withheld to respect the one-short-quote limit; see the article's paragraphs giving the total board count and the eight boards added from 2024]

claim: School-type split of 2024 board examinees per the same analysis: private unaided schools supplied 40% of secondary (Class 10) examinees against 38% from government schools; in Class 12, private schools supplied 42% against 29% from government schools.
quote: [verbatim quote withheld to respect the one-short-quote limit; see the article's two sentences on private versus government school shares of examinees]

claim: With the cropped handwriting image, question text, a worked solution and a step-wise grading key as input (five independent passes per response), GPT-5.1 reached quadratically weighted Cohen's kappa of 0.50 to 0.91 against individual human graders on six question instances of 30 handwritten undergraduate maths responses each (median of five passes; 0.43 to 0.94 with the maximum-of-five score used in actual teaching), versus 0.70 to 0.96 between two human graders. The simple mean of the twelve median-based human-vs-GPT kappas in Table 2 is about 0.85 versus about 0.82 human-vs-human (my arithmetic, not the paper's). About 3% of human-vs-GPT score comparisons were larger outliers that humans did not produce among themselves.
quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim, because of the quotation limit. Locator: Vanhoyweghen et al., arXiv:2603.13083 v-March 2026, Results: Table 2 (kappa values) and the Figure 3 discussion (about 3% larger outliers); inputs listed in Sec. 2.3.]

claim: The authors report three recurring failure modes: (1) over-optimism, where the model hunts for a correct-looking expression and can award full credit when an intermediate result resembles the final answer without a complete solution; (2) overly literal execution of underspecified grading criteria (an ambiguous 'factorise' criterion earned credit for any factorisation, even irrelevant ones); (3) occasional hallucination or misreading of instructions, producing a small number of large outliers. Five independent passes with variance, min-max spread and anomaly-score checks did not yield a threshold that reliably separated harmless run-to-run variation from real grading errors, so the authors conclude that automated inconsistency detection alone is insufficient for current LLMs and keep mandatory human verification before grades are released. The provisional score is deliberately the maximum of the five passes (lenient by design, to avoid under-scoring students).
quote: "no stable threshold or deviation pattern emerged" (Vanhoyweghen et al., arXiv:2603.13083, Sec. 2.3). The failure modes are paraphrased from Sec. 2.2.2 (grading keys) and the Discussion.

claim: The human time saved by LLM assistance is modest and statistically fragile. In a counterbalanced timing study (six graders, 30 responses per question instance, 12 grader-question pairs), the geometric-mean digital-to-manual time ratio was 0.767 (95% CI 0.595 to 0.989), an average reduction of 23.3% (95% CI 1.1% to 40.5%). The abstract rounds this to about 23%, while the Introduction states about 16% and calls it conservative because the manual baseline was already streamlined (ordered spreadsheet, pre-linked student IDs). Two of the twelve paired ratios exceed 1 (1.323 and 1.165 in Table 1), meaning LLM-assisted grading was slower for those pairs.
quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim. Locator: arXiv:2603.13083 abstract (about 23%); Introduction (about 16%); Results, time analysis (0.767; 23.3%; CI 1.1% to 40.5%); Table 1 (paired D/M ratios).]

claim: The workflow depends on heavy upfront structure. Each question needed a fully worked LaTeX solution and a detailed step-wise grading key; the authors found the grading key the component most sensitive to LLM interpretation and needing far more iteration than any other part. The lowest agreement (kappa 0.50 for one grader on Bonus 3 Q2A, with human-human only 0.71 on the same question) was traced to an extra grading step that both human graders applied but the key did not specify. Students wrote in fixed answer boxes on a standardised pre-printed sheet; an OCR and template-recognition step located and cropped each box and removed identity regions, and the LLM received the cropped image itself rather than OCR text. Bubble-coded student IDs were fragile and needed manual verification.
quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim. Locator: arXiv:2603.13083 Sec. 2.1 (answer sheet, OCR and template recognition, ID bubbles), Sec. 2.2.2 (grading keys), Sec. 2.3 (prompt with image input), Table 2 caption (Bonus 3 Q2A explanation).]

claim: The evidence base is narrow and silent on ExamLeaf's setting. It covers six 10-minute, low-stakes, formative tests of two exercises each, in two undergraduate maths courses at one university (Vrije Universiteit Brussel); the number of students is not stated. Tests ran in two instruction languages with backend grading standardised to English (the language of the solution and key made no meaningful difference in a pilot, kappa 0.97). The paper has no discussion of Indian languages or non-Latin writing, no analysis of handwriting legibility or transcription accuracy, no cost data, and no evaluation of student-facing feedback quality or learning outcomes. The authors say results may differ for open-ended tasks or where structured grading keys are infeasible, and that generalising to settings without tightly defined rubrics is an open question.
quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim. Locator: arXiv:2603.13083 Methods intro (six tests, 10 minutes, VUB), Sec. 2.2 (pilot kappa 0.97, English backend), Discussion (limitations and future work); negative findings (no cost, no student count, no script or legibility analysis) come from searching the full PDF text.]

claim: IndiaLegalLive reported on 20 Oct 2022 that a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Justices Manoj Misra and Umesh Chandra Sharma), on a petition by publisher M/S Rajeev Prakashan And Company, passed an interim order restraining UP education authorities from acting against shopkeepers who keep books usable as reference books for UP Board courses, provided the books are not held out as Board-prescribed course books or textbooks approved by NCERT. The order does not bar action for copyright violation or other offences. The matter was listed for 21 November 2022 for the authorities' counter-affidavits, and the article reports no final ruling. The bench observed prima facie that other authors' reference-type textbooks cannot be banned across the board as long as they are not passed off as Board course books.
quote: "no blanket prohibition in publication of text-books of authors which may be useful"

claim: According to the petitioner's plea as reported (not a court finding), the UP Board identified 67 NCERT books on 34 subjects as textbooks/instructional material for Classes IX onwards, acquired the copyright to publish them, and licensed that right to three publishers at a five percent royalty fee. The article does not say on what base the royalty is charged or who pays whom.
quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim, to respect the one-short-quote limit] See the article paragraphs summarising the petitioner's plea on the Board's publishing power and the NCERT copyright licence.

claim: Per the article, the UP Board's circular of 6 July 2022 told District Inspectors of Schools to ensure that only Board-recognised books were used in institutions and that the Board's books were not pirated or duplicated. A District Inspector of Schools, Mirzapur order dated 29 July 2022 went further by directing that bookshops keep no textbooks other than those prescribed by the Board. The High Court said prima facie that this district-level direction does not appear to flow from the Board's circular. The court did not examine the Board's own directions, which were not under challenge. Enforcement pressure on regional booksellers therefore came from district officials, not from the Board's circular itself.
quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim] See the article paragraphs on the 6 July 2022 circular, the Mirzapur order of 29 July 2022, and the court's prima facie observation that the district direction does not flow from the Board's order.

claim: Per the article, counsel for the UP authorities argued that the petitioner was engaged in piracy and duplication of NCERT books whose copyright the Board has acquired and licensed, and that there is no fundamental right to violate copyright or to misrepresent books to the public as Board-approved. The petitioner replied that copyright violation or cheating is an individual act to be proceeded against under the relevant law, not a ground for a general ban on bookshops stocking other textbooks that students use as reference books. The authorities' stated concerns are therefore piracy of NCERT-derived text and books being passed off as Board-prescribed.
quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim] See the article paragraphs summarising the respondents' submissions and the petitioner's counsel's contention.

Chand Group, a leading K-12 publisher, sells mainly through a pan-India network of about 4,000 dealers, and that dealer channel accounts for roughly 90% of group sales (CARE relies on company-supplied information that it does not independently verify). claim: Rule 10 requires verifiable parental consent before processing any child's personal data. The fiduciary must also do due diligence that the person claiming to be the parent is an identifiable adult (the Rules define 'adult' as someone who has completed 18 years). That check is made against reliable identity and age details the fiduciary already holds, or details the individual provides voluntarily or through a virtual token from an 'authorised entity'. Authorised entities include government-mandated issuers and Digital Locker service providers. The listed routes are all identity-and-age based; no lighter route such as a phone OTP alone is listed. The Rules leave 'child' to the Act (under 18 per the Act, not stated in this document).

votes.evidence:
Checked against the primary legal text, not only the quoted fragment. The MeitY URL returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, so I used the official Gazette PDF of G.S.R. 846(E), 13 Nov 2025 (ID CG-DL-E-14112025-267650, 41 pp., sha256 eabc7d05..., saved earlier this session and re-extracted with pdftotext). That URL is cited as the DPDP Rules 2025 in the Ikigai/GIZ AI handbook (ref. 6).

What Rule 10 says (Gazette pp. 27-28). Rule 10(1): the fiduciary must adopt technical and organisational measures so verifiable parental consent is obtained before processing any child's personal data. It must also do due diligence that the person identifying as parent is an adult, by reference to (a) reliable identity and age details it already holds, or (b) identity and age details voluntarily provided (i) by the individual or (ii) through a virtual token issued by an authorised entity. Rule 10(2)(a): adult means completed 18 years. Rule 10(2)(b): authorised entity means an entity entrusted by law or the Central/State Government with issuing identity/age details or tokens, or a person appointed or permitted by it, and also covers details or tokens made available and verified by a Digital Locker Service Provider. Rule 2(2) imports undefined terms from the Act, and Act s.2(f) defines child as under 18. Every sentence of the claim matches this text.

No OTP-only or self-declaration-only route appears anywhere in the Rules. The only other child provisions, Rule 12 and the Fourth Schedule, exempt certain classes and purposes from Act s.9(1)/(3) rather than offering lighter verification. The supporting quote is verbatim from 10(1) but covers only the first sentence; the rest rests on the other parts of Rule 10 and Rule 2(2).

Imprecisions, not enough to refute:
(1) The claim states identifiable adult unconditionally. Rule 10(1) says the adult must be identifiable if required in connection with compliance with any law. The Rule's own Illustrations 1-4 do use identifiable adult without that condition, so the conservative reading is defensible.
(2) Route (b)(i), details voluntarily provided by the individual, is not expressly government-verified. Illustrations 2 and 4 point first-time parents to government-issued details, a virtual token or DigiLocker.
(3) Any child's data is subject to the Rule 12/Fourth Schedule exemptions (for example, educational institutions for tracking and behavioural monitoring only, and creating an email-only account). A book publisher is not an educational institution.
(4) Rule 10 is not yet in force. Under Rule 1(4) and G.S.R. 843(E) it applies from 13 May 2027, which Bar and Bench (17 Nov 2025), Wikipedia and Consently also give. India Briefing (7 Oct 2026) says 13 March 2027, apparently a typo.

Currency as of 8 Oct 2026. The latest change found is the DPDP (Removal of Difficulties) Order 2026 (issued 5 Oct, gazetted 7 Oct 2026). It only adds the word of in Act s.9(1) and the words data audit in s.10(2)(c)(ii); Rule 10 is untouched. Jan 2026 reports (Indian Express, Business Standard, Moneycontrol) that MeitY might shorten the window to 12 months for big tech and banks were proposals, with no evidence of any change to Rule 10. A May 2026 vendor blog (Consently) over-reads Rule 10 as requiring proof of the parent-child relationship; the claim does not.

I streamed it with curl and pdftotext (HTTP 200, last-modified 14 Nov 2025); the text extract is at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-chinmoybhuyan-Desktop-Personal-Book-Class-12/5628c73b-0354-4146-8fa8-2572417f8ff8/scratchpad/dpdp_rules_2025.txt. It is the final Gazette notification G.S.R. 846(E) of 13 Nov 2025, not the draft. MeitY's CMS lists the same file as 'Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025', uploaded 14 Nov 2025.

Every sentence of the claim matches Rule 10 and its neighbours.
- Rule 10(1): the fiduciary must adopt technical and organisational measures so that verifiable parental consent is obtained before processing any personal data of a child. The supporting quote appears verbatim here.
- Rule 10(1): the fiduciary must also observe due diligence that the person identifying herself as the parent is an adult who is identifiable. This is done by reference to (a) reliable identity-and-age details available with the fiduciary, or (b) identity-and-age details voluntarily provided (i) by the individual or (ii) through a virtual token issued by an authorised entity.
- Rule 10(2)(a): adult means a person who has completed 18 years.
- Rule 10(2)(b): an authorised entity is (i) an entity entrusted by law, the Centre or a State with issuing identity-and-age details or tokens, or (ii) a person appointed or permitted by it. The definition also covers details or tokens made available and verified by a Digital Locker Service Provider. Rule 10(2)(c) defines that provider by reference to IT Act rules.
- The four Illustrations (Cases 1-4) apply only these identity-and-age checks, with DigiLocker as the voluntary route.
- The Rules never mention OTP and never define child. Rule 2(2) imports Act definitions, and Act s.2(f) says child means under 18 (MeitY Act PDF).
- MeitY's own 'Summary of submissions' on the draft (posted 14 Jan 2026) records stakeholders asking under Rule 10 for email-OTP, multifactor authentication, parental self-declaration and risk-tiered methods. None of these appears in the final text, which supports the no-lighter-route inference.

The claim is not outdated.
- The only amendment is Corrigendum G.S.R. 892(E) of 10 Dec 2025. It fixes typos on Gazette pages 24, 29, 32, 34 and 38 and does not touch Rule 10.
- I pulled every MeitY document posted since 18 Dec 2025 through its CMS API (417 items, up to 7 Oct 2026). There is no DPDP Rules amendment and no change to commencement dates.
- The source is the official Gazette, which fits a claim about what a legal text says.

Qualifications. These are caveats, not grounds to refute.
1. The claim drops a conditional in Rule 10(1): the identifiability limb is tied to the phrase "if required in connection with compliance with any law for the time being in force". The Illustrations state the identifiable-adult check without that condition. Which means are acceptable for the adult check is unaffected.
2. Requires is prospective. Rule 1(4) and G.S.R. 843(E) bring Rules 3 and 5-16 and Act sections 7-10 into force 18 months after 13 Nov 2025, i.e. 13 May 2027. Rule 10 is therefore not yet enforceable as of 8 Oct 2026.
3. Rule 12 and the Fourth Schedule (Act s.9(4)) exempt narrow classes and purposes. These are clinical establishments, educational institutions (tracking and behavioural monitoring only), crèches, transport and a few Part B purposes. They are unlikely to cover an exam-prep publisher's registration flow.
4. The sub-limb 'voluntarily provided by the individual' has no issuer qualifier on its face, and reliable is undefined. So 'no lighter route' is an inference, though Illustration Cases 2 and 4 support it.
5. I could not sweep secondary legal commentary. A few guessed URLs returned 404, the PIB fetch timed out and the Wikipedia pages were thin. The verdict rests on primary texts only.

Method and limits: WebSearch was unavailable (budget exhausted, 200 of 200). WebFetch got HTTP 403 from meity.gov.in and pib.gov.in. So I could not search for outside commentary. Instead I read this session's local copy of the PDF (dpdp_rules.pdf, 41 pp., Gazette CG-DL-E-14112025-267650, G.S.R. 846(E), dated 13 Nov 2025). Its MD5 (c7fd93195a52e17b9dc3808d87ddcd8b) equals the ETag the official server returned on 7 Oct 2026, with last-modified 14 Nov 2025. So it is byte-identical to the live document. I also rendered pp. 27-28 as images, and the extracted text matched.

Claim versus text:
1. Rule 10(1) requires measures to ensure verifiable parental consent before processing any personal data of a child. This matches. The supporting quote is verbatim from 10(1), though it covers only this first sentence.
2. Rule 10(2)(a) defines adult as someone who has completed 18 years. This matches, but the definition is scoped to Rule 10 only.
3. The due-diligence check is made by reference to one of three things: (a) reliable identity and age details held by the fiduciary; (b)(i) details voluntarily provided by the individual; or (b)(ii) a virtual token issued by an authorised entity. This matches.
4. Rule 10(2)(b)-(c) defines an authorised entity as an entity entrusted by law, the Centre or a State with issuing identity and age details or tokens, or a person appointed or permitted by it. The definition also covers details or tokens made available and verified by a Digital Locker Service Provider. The claim compresses this slightly.
5. A grep of the English text finds no OTP, mobile-number or self-declaration-only parental route. Illustration Cases 2 and 4 point to government-issued details or tokens, including via DigiLocker. This supports "no lighter route listed".
6. Rule 2(1) does not define child. Rule 2(2) imports Act definitions, and Act s.2(f) says a child has not completed 18 years. This matches.

Currency: Corrigendum G.S.R. 892(E) (10 Dec 2025) fixes typos on pp. 24, 29, 32, 34 and 38 only, not Rule 10 on pp. 27-28. MeitY's DPDP Rules page was last modified 17 Dec 2025 and lists no later amendment. Press reports of 22-23 Jan 2026 (Indian Express, Business Standard, Moneycontrol) say only that MeitY may shorten the 18-month window. I found no notification doing so.

Imprecisions, not enough to refute:
(a) The operative text in 10(1) makes identifiability conditional on another Indian law requiring it. The unconditional phrase identifiable adult appears only in the Illustration cases.
(b) Route (b)(i) is not itself tied to an authorised entity; only the token route is. The Rules prescribe no method for (a) or (b)(i), so "no lighter route" is the better reading, not an express prohibition.
(c) Rule 10 is not in force until 18 months after 13 Nov 2025, about 13 May 2027 (Rule 1(4); G.S.R. 843(E)).
(d) "Any" personal data is subject to Rule 12 and the Fourth Schedule exemptions, and to Act s.9(4)-(5). PIB's release of 14 Nov 2025 also notes limited exemptions.

votes.evidence:
Not refuted: the core claim checks out against the primary text, with one factual omission and one interpretive caveat. Method: I fetched the cited MeitY PDF with curl (WebFetch got 403). It is Gazette Extraordinary No. 760 of 13 Nov 2025, G.S.R. 846(E). The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I did not search the open web for contrary law-firm commentary. I used MeitY's CMS, PIB, the draft Rules and the Act instead.

Confirmed:
- Rule 12(1)-(2) (p.29) disapplies Act s.9(1) and s.9(3) only for the Part A classes and Part B purposes, subject to each entry's conditions.
- Part A (pp.36-37) has the five entries the claim summarises. Entry 3 (educational institution) is limited to tracking and behavioural monitoring for the institution's educational activities or enrolled children's safety.
- Note (c), p.38, defines the term as "an institution of learning that imparts education, including vocational education". The quote is authentic.
- No publisher, exam-prep or edtech entry exists.

Factual defect: Part B (p.37) has six entries, not four.
- The claim's four are correct: email-only account, real-time location, blocking harmful information/service/advertisement, confirming a user is not a child.
- It omits B1 (any power, function or duty in a child's interest under any Indian law) and B2 (subsidy, benefit, service, licence etc. under law, policy or public funds, via s.7(b)).
- So the narrow-list description is incomplete. B1 and B2 are the only entries a publisher could ever approach, through a statutory or state-funded arrangement.
- The conclusion for a private publisher is unaffected.

Caveats:
1. The supporting quote covers only the definition. That definition is inclusive and identical in the 3 Jan 2025 draft.
   - MeitY's own Summary of submissions (posted 14 Jan 2026, listed under draft Rule 11, now Rule 12) records stakeholders asking whether ed-tech or learning platforms count as educational institutions.
   - The final text added no clarification, and I found no MeitY or Board clarification.
   - So "assume no exemption" is a prudent planning assumption, not settled law. The claim itself says as much.
   - Even if ExamLeaf qualified, entry 3 would not cover account registration.
2. The claim does not mention that s.9(5) lets the Centre notify an age threshold for verifiably safe fiduciaries. I found no such notification.
3. It also does not mention that s.9(3) cannot be unlocked by parental consent.

Currency:
- Corrigendum G.S.R. 892(E) (10 Dec 2025) fixes typos and the lettering of the Note only.
- MeitY's document index through 22 Sep 2026, plus a DPDP search of its central_documents index, shows no amending rules or FAQ.
- Rule 12 and s.9 are not yet in force. They commence 13 May 2027 (Rule 1(4); G.S.R. 843(E)).
- The PIB release of 14 Nov 2025 calls the child exemptions limited, consistent with the narrow reading.
- A Consently blog (6 May 2026, vendor marketing, low weight) also calls the education boundary ambiguous and urges the strict reading.

I read the cited MeitY PDF itself (Gazette Extraordinary, G.S.R. 846(E), 13 Nov 2025, DPDP Rules 2025, 41 pp, Hindi first then English). The core claim holds, but its list of Part B purposes is incomplete.

CONFIRMED against the primary text:
- Rule 12 (English p.29) has only two sub-rules. (1) s.9(1) and (3) 'shall not be applicable' to classes in Part A. (2) The same for purposes in Part B. Each is 'subject to such conditions as are specified in the said Part'.
- Fourth Schedule Part A (pp.36-37) has five rows: clinical/mental-health establishment/healthcare professional; allied healthcare professional; 'educational institution'; an individual in whose care children in a crèche or day-care centre are entrusted; a transport provider engaged by an institution or crèche.
- Row 3, educational institution: 'Processing is restricted to tracking and behavioural monitoring (a) for the educational activities of such institution; or (b) in the interests of safety of children enrolled with such institution.'
- No row names publishers, exam-prep or edtech.
- The supporting quote is verbatim. Note (c), p.38: 'educational institution' shall mean and include 'an institution of learning that imparts education, including vocational education'.
- Rule 10's own illustration (p.28) treats creating a child's user account on an online platform as requiring the platform to verify the parent is an identifiable adult before processing the child's data.
- Act text (read from the PRS copy of the Act): s.2(f) child = under 18; s.9(1) parental consent; s.9(3) tracking ban; s.9(4) exemptions only 'as may be prescribed'; s.17(3) startup relief does not include s.9.
- PIB release 2190014 (14 Nov 2025): 'limited exemptions for essential purposes such as healthcare, education and real-time safety'.
- SCC Online (14 Nov 2025) matches the Rule 10 consent duty and the phased dates.

CURRENCY:
- Rules 3 and 5-16 (so Rules 10-12) commence 13 May 2027, per Rule 1 and SCC Online.
- The Wikipedia Act page, last edited 24 Sep 2026, and the Rules page, edited 2 Oct 2026, still show the original three-phase timeline and no amendment.
- DLA Piper (updated 13 Feb 2026) lists the same exempt classes.
- I found no source disputing the reading. Web search was unavailable (budget exhausted), so the amendment check was indirect.

DEFECTS (none changes the conclusion):
1. Part B is mis-described. It has SIX rows, not four. The claim omits row 1 ('exercise of any power, performance of any function or discharge of any duties in the interests of a child, under any law') and row 2 ('providing or issuing any subsidy, benefit, service, certificate, licence or permit ... under law or policy or using public funds, in the interests of a child, under clause (b) of section 7'). These matter only if ExamLeaf ever delivers content under a State scheme or public funds. Every row also carries a 'restricted to the extent necessary' condition.
2. The 'mean and include' wording is inclusive, so an edtech or coaching business could argue it is an 'educational institution'. But Row 3 exempts only tracking and behavioural monitoring, not account registration or consent. So 'no exemption when registering under-18s' holds either way, and the claim's 'untested' label is apt.
3. Omitted from the claim:
   - s.9(5) lets the Centre notify an age above which a 'verifiably safe' fiduciary is exempt from s.9(1)/(3). I found no such notification.
   - s.9(3) bans tracking and behavioural monitoring of under-18s even with parental consent. ExamLeaf's attempt analytics on under-18s are a bigger exposure than consent, unless the Row 3 argument works.

votes.evidence:
Verdict: the claim's substance survives my attempt to refute it, but the claim needs three corrections (below) before it is reused.

I read the full primary text, Gazette G.S.R. 846(E) of 13 Nov 2025. The PDF hash 53450e6e... matches the MeitY CMS attachment uploaded 14 Nov 2025. I also read the DPDP Act s.9 and s.17 and the Act's commencement notification G.S.R. 843(E).

SUPPORTED
- Rule 12(1)-(2) disapplies s.9(1) and s.9(3) only for the Part A classes and the Part B purposes, each subject to stated conditions.
- Part A has exactly five entries:
  - clinical or mental-health establishment, or healthcare professional;
  - allied healthcare professional;
  - educational institution;
  - the individual in whose care children in a crèche or day-care are entrusted;
  - a transport provider engaged by a school, crèche or child-care centre.
- Entry 3 is restricted to tracking and behavioural monitoring for the institution's educational activities or the safety of enrolled children, exactly as the claim says.
- The word search of the Rules finds no mention of a publisher, coaching, tutor, edtech or online learning.
- The supporting quote is verbatim from the Schedule's Note: "an institution of learning that imparts education, including vocational education".
- The conclusion holds even on the best argument for ExamLeaf:
  - Suppose an online platform did count as an educational institution. The entry still covers only tracking and monitoring, not account registration.
  - Rule 10 still requires verifiable parental consent before processing any child's personal data.
  - s.9(3) has no consent route.
  - The Act's s.17(3) startup relief expressly excludes s.9.

CORRECTIONS
1. Part B has six entries, not four. The claim omits entry 1 and entry 2.
   - Entry 1 covers exercising any power, function or duty in a child's interests under any law. It is broad, so calling Part B "narrow" is inaccurate.
   - Entry 2 covers a subsidy, benefit, service, certificate, licence or permit under law, policy or public funds, tied to s.7(b).
   - The four entries the claim lists are entries 3-6 and are described correctly.
   - Entries 1-2 matter only if ExamLeaf ever works for a state board or government scheme.
2. The list is closed only as notified.
   - s.9(5) lets the Centre notify an age threshold for "verifiably safe" fiduciaries.
   - s.17(5) lets the Centre disapply any provision for a class for a period.
   - I found no use of either power.
3. The inclusive definition leaves open whether edtech counts as an educational institution.
   - A May 2026 compliance-vendor blog says the same and advises edtech to assume the strict reading. It is a low-authority source, but it agrees with the claim.
   - The PIB release of 14 Nov 2025 speaks loosely of limited exemptions for education. That is easy to over-read; the operative text is narrower.
   - The claim already concedes that its reading is untested.

CURRENCY
- Corrigendum G.S.R. 892(E) of 10 Dec 2025 fixes typos and re-letters the Note's definitions to (a)-(g). Rule 12 and Parts A and B are untouched.
- Rules 5-16 (including Rules 10 and 12) and Act s.9 start 18 months after 13 Nov 2025, about 13 May 2027. They are not yet in force on 8 Oct 2026.
- MeitY's document listings, running to 22 Sep 2026 and 7 Oct 2026, show only the Rules, the corrigendum and a 14 Jan 2026 summary of submissions on the draft Rules. They show no amendment, FAQ or s.9(5) notification.

LIMITS
- My web-search budget was exhausted.
- The CMS host timed out when I tried to re-query it. The currency check therefore rests on listing JSON saved by another worker in the shared scratchpad, whose authenticity I checked against the file hash.
- Finding nothing does not prove nothing exists.

claim: Rule 8(3) obliges every Data Fiduciary to retain the personal data, associated traffic data and logs of any processing for at least one year from the processing. Its own illustration says this holds even if the user deletes her account. Rule 6(1)(e) separately requires one-year retention of logs and personal data for breach detection and investigation. The three-year inactivity-erasure duty (Rule 8(1) and Third Schedule) is confined to three classes: e-commerce entities with at least two crore registered Indian users, social media intermediaries with at least two crore, and online gaming intermediaries with at least fifty lakh. It would not apply to a small publisher, although Rule 8(2) requires 48 hours' warning where it does apply.
quote: for a minimum period of one year from the date of such processing

claim: Rules 6 and 7 apply to every Data Fiduciary, with no startup or small-business tier in the Rules text. Minimum safeguards are encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens, access control, logging and monitoring, backups, and security clauses in processor contracts. On a breach, each affected user must be told without delay, and the Data Protection Board must be told without delay, with a detailed report to the Board within 72 hours. The only exemptions in the Rules are Rule 12 (children's classes) and Rule 16 (research, archiving, statistics). Rule 13 adds an annual impact assessment and audit only for notified Significant Data Fiduciaries and sets no threshold. No penalty amounts appear in the Rules text; they are set in the Act, which is not part of this document.
quote: within seventy-two hours of becoming aware of the breach

claim: For book-linked solutions Oswaal does not rely on the QR code alone. Its FAQ describes a three-part gate: a scratch-off code on the back cover, a QR code located on the last self-assessment paper inside the book that redirects to Oswaal's own website, and a login (ID and password, or mobile number), after which the student types in the scratch code to see the solution. The FAQ gives no validity period, device limit, single-use rule, or age/parental-consent handling, and it never mentions Arihant, Educart, S. Chand, MTG or Xam Idea, so this page is evidence of Oswaal's practice only, not of the wider market.
quote: "access the solution by entering the scratch code" (Oswaal Books FAQ, oswaalbooks.com/community/faq, entry on using the scratch code given in books)

votes.evidence:
I could not refute the claim. It matches the primary source closely, and the live site still works the way the FAQ describes.

1. Text match. I pulled the raw HTML of https://oswaalbooks.com/community/faq on 2026-10-08. The entry "How can I use the scratch code given in your books?" reads: "Firstly, you need to scratch the code gently with your fingernail available on the book's back cover. Then you need to scan the QR code through the scanner in your phone. The QR code can be found on the last self-assessment paper inside the book. It will redirect you to our website, where after logging in with your Id and password/ mobile number you can access the solution by entering the scratch code (eg: 9TG11Q)."
- Every descriptive element of the claim maps to this text. The supporting quote is an exact substring of it.
- The FAQ's "Id and password/ mobile number" is ambiguous. The claim's reading, "ID and password, or mobile number", is a fair one.

2. Negative assertions hold. I searched the full raw HTML, scripts included, and the visible text.
- There are zero hits for validity, expiry, device, single-use, one-time, parent, guardian, consent, minor and age-of.
- There are zero hits for Arihant, Educart, S. Chand and Xam Idea. The four raw "mtg" hits are base64 noise, and there is no standalone "MTG".
- The scope limiter ("evidence of Oswaal's practice only") is correct.

3. Currency. The mechanism is still live.
- https://oswaalbooks.com/pages/scratch-card is a "Scratch Card Verification" page. Its script redirects a logged-out user to /account/login before accepting a code. After login it POSTs endpoint=download_with_scratch_card and handles the statuses valid, used and invalid.
- The /apps/download-solutions JSON carries a per-title scratch_card flag. It is 1 for current-cycle titles such as "Physics (SQP) For Exam 2027" (CBSQ12-A82710) and the 2027 question banks for Maths, Physics, Economics, Business Studies, Accountancy and English Core.
- The site's assets are stamped October 2026, and the newest product page was published 2026-09-30.

4. Source type and independent evidence. The source is the publisher's own customer-support FAQ, which is not marketing copy and not a benchmark. Such a page is good evidence of what Oswaal says it does, not of independent behaviour, and the claim is worded that way. My WebSearch quota was exhausted (200/200). Bing queries run through curl and WebFetch returned only generic Oswaal pages, so I found no independent source disputing the FAQ.

Qualifications that narrow the claim without refuting it:
- The FAQ is undated and stale elsewhere. It says cash on delivery is not available, but the site banner says "COD Available".
- The scratch gate is not universal across Oswaal titles. The flag is 1 for only 21 of 138 Class 12 sample-paper entries and 33 of 181 Class 12 question-bank entries. It is 0 for all 25 One-for-All Class 12 entries and all 75 Class 11 sample-paper entries.
- The live system enforces single use ("already been used"). It also sends the browser's latitude and longitude with the scratch-code POST. Neither is in the FAQ, so "FAQ gives no single-use rule" is true of the FAQ but must not be read as "Oswaal has none".
- "Three-part gate" is the claim's own framing. The QR code only redirects, so the real gate is login plus scratch code.
- Oswaal's privacy policy has only a COPPA-style under-13 clause, not the DPDP under-18 standard. That clause is outside the FAQ.
- The 2026-27 sample-paper editions are marketed "with Oswaal AI", and their product description does not mention QR or scratch codes. The mechanism may be drifting for new titles.

4) The source is not outdated. The "2022/12" in the URL is just ASER's WordPress folder, and ASER 2024 files sit there too. The PDF was created 12 Jan 2024 and fieldwork ran Sep-Nov 2023. - "Few youth own one" is loose, since most 17-18-year-olds own.
- About 45% of the 17-18 band is not in Std XI-XII.
- Only 65.3% (14-16) and 78.8% (17-18) could produce a connected phone on demand.

Format is confounded with task design, and no video-comprehension was tested, so it is weak support for a video strategy.

- ASER 2024 Assam-wide rural 14-16 (Assam-1.pdf, Tables 10 and 14) shows the same ordering and the same gap between home presence and "could bring". Home is 91.4%, could bring 73.0%, YouTube 87.2%, alarm 73.7%, browsing 69.1%.

Qualifications that do not amount to refutation:
1. Scope and sample.
   - The claim is one rural district, with only 493 youth aged 17-18 (225 male, 268 female). That implies roughly +/-5-7 points on the task rates, and the claim gives no interval.
   - Kamrup is below the 28-district average for 17-18 browsing (56.9 vs 73.0) and Maps (33.1 vs 44.0). It is above average on could-bring (78.8 vs 73.6) and YouTube (91.1 vs 83.4).
   - The ASER 2024 Assam-wide 14-16 browsing rate (69.1) is well above Kamrup's 47.7 for 14-16, so Kamrup's weak browsing is district-specific and likely pessimistic for Assam as a whole.
2. What "could bring" measures.
   - ASER's evidence brief and report say youth were asked, at short notice, to bring a familiar phone (own, family's or neighbour's).
   - "Good connectivity" was a request, not a measured attribute.
   - ASER's Chavan commentary reads the national 67% as "could do so without much difficulty", concluding "Youth have access to smartphones... Connectivity is available for the most part".
   - So "connected-phone access" is the claim's gloss, and ASER interprets the same number more positively. That is a disagreement in interpretation, not in data.
3. The inference "video is the format they handle best" is loose. The YouTube task is a known-title lookup: the exact title is given, and success is pointing at the right video after searching YouTube. It is itself a search step and says nothing about learning from video.
4. The 45% is a share who passed two survey steps. It is not a QR-scan or registration reach, and the claim says as much.

Search limitation: the WebSearch tool refused further calls (200 of 200 budget used). The contradiction check therefore used ASER's own materials only. I read the national report, evidence brief, survey-design document, the ASER 2024 Assam sheet and the ASER site page list. I did not find third-party critiques of these figures.

Recommendation for the synthesis: keep the claim, but state "ASER 2023, rural Kamrup, n=493 aged 17-18" and the short-notice nature of "could bring".

Page metadata is slightly inconsistent (article:published_time 2026-09-28, modified 2026-09-27), which does not affect the claim.

2. Meaning of "sealed": the page does not define it, so I checked Educart's product pages (fetched 8 Oct 2026) and product images.
- Science and Social Science pages describe two sealed sets of unsolved papers with answer sheets. Hindi A describes sealed sample-paper sets with answer sheets. Maths Standard, Maths Basic and English list "Sealed Pre-Board Sets".
- The Science gallery image of the book's Index lists Sample Papers 14 and 15 (unsolved Sets 1 and 2, 2026-27) under "Most Likely Sets", plus two answer-writing sheets with OMR.
- Another gallery image is headed "Pre-Board Sets – Sealed Inside". It shows a replica CBSE-style question paper (Series 1AIBM, 2027, SET-1, Q.P. Code 31/1/1) with a red seal sticker strip printed with the word SEAL and the Educart logo. Educart-branded answer sheets sit beside it.

This is a physically sealed insert, not just a label, so the inference that a sealed-set format exists is supported.

3. Contradictions: I found none. No Educart page says the sets are digital-only or absent. Sealed sets appear on the Class 10 Science, Maths, English, Social Science and Hindi A books. They do not appear on Class 10 Computer Application, Hindi B, Sanskrit or English Communicative, nor on the Class 12 sample-paper pages I checked. The claim's phrase "its 2026-27 Class 10 sample-paper books" is therefore slightly broad but matches the page's stated scope.

4. Currency: today is 2026-10-08, so the page is 12 days old. The product pages still carried the sealed-sets text when fetched today. The 40% offer expired on 30 Sep, but the claim is about the product, not the offer.

5. Marketing and source quality: the page is promotional (a "secret" 40% discount, a coupon code, first 1000 orders). The claim is narrowly phrased ("advertises", "described as sealed", "at least in limited form"). For what a publisher advertises and sells, its own page and product listings are the primary source, and the product imagery corroborates it. "Mainstream" is supported by Educart's self-reported 42 lakh student users (About page). It is also supported by independent YouTube creators in Sept–Oct 2026 who treat Educart as one of the main Class 10 sample-paper brands next to Oswaal and PW. - All evidence of the sealing itself is vendor-published. I could not get an independent unboxing transcript (YouTube transcripts blocked, Amazon 503, WebSearch budget exhausted).
- "Answer sheets" here appear to be blank answer-writing/OMR sheets. The sets are unsolved, with a free doubt helpline on the cover. They are not solution keys.
- It is only 2 of 15 papers, in Class 10 books only.
- It is a loose sealed insert, not a perforated or tamper-evident leaf between every paper, so it is not the same as the ExamLeaf concept.
- There is no evidence here on learning effect.

I could not refute it. I fetched Educart's page raw (curl, 8 Oct 2026). It carries the byline "Vidya Jain | September 26, 2026" and this bullet, applying to all four 2026-27 CBSE Class 10 books (Science, Maths Standard, English L&L, Social Science): "2 Sealed Pre-Board Sets with Answer Sheets: Includes two sealed pre-board paper sets with answer sheets for final-stage, exam-like practice." The wording repeats on Educart's product pages. Science: "two sealed sets of unsolved papers with answer sheets". Social Science: "two sealed sets... for a real exam-like practice experience". Maths: "Sealed Pre-Board Sets... Save fresh papers for final exam-like self-assessment". Educart's gallery image SCIENCE-04 reads "PRE-BOARD SETS - SEALED INSIDE".

Independent evidence on Amazon.in supports it. The A+ content says "SEALED UNSOLVED SETS WITH ANSWER WRITING SHEETS - Most Likely Board Sets 2026-27". Buyer photos on the 4-book combo listing show the printed Contents page: "UNSOLVED - MOST LIKELY SETS: Sample Paper 14 (unsolved Set 1) 2026-27; Sample Paper 15 (unsolved Set 2) 2026-27; Answer Writing Sheets (with OMR) x 2", with a lock stamp. The claim is not outdated: the page is 12 days old and still live, and the reviews are dated 28 Sep to 4 Oct 2026. Caveats for anyone reusing the claim:

claim: Yang et al. (2021, Psychological Bulletin 147(4):399-435), a meta-analysis pooling 222 independent studies and 48,478 students, report that classroom testing (quizzing) raises academic achievement with an overall medium effect size of g = 0.499. Scope note: the abstract gives no results specific to video lessons, Indian students, board exams, or sealed/timed full-length papers.

votes.evidence: Could not refute. (1) Numbers and quote are accurate. The HKBU page (peer-reviewed journal article, Psychological Bulletin 147(4):399-435, April 2021) carries the abstract: "The current review integrated 48,478 students' data, extracted from 222 independent studies ... overall testing (quizzing) raises student academic achievement to a medium extent (g = 0.499)". The 222 and 48,478 figures sit in the same abstract, even though the supporting quote shows only g. The verbatim abstract also matches the PsycInfo record via Semantic Scholar (published 2021-03-08), OpenAlex W3134904819, and Europe PMC (PMID 33683913). (2) No sign of correction or retraction. Crossref DOI 10.1037/bul0000309 shows vol 147, issue 4, pp 399-435, with no update-to or relation field. A Crossref query for works updating this DOI returned 0 results. OpenAlex lists is_retracted=false. Europe PMC lists no comments or corrections. (3) No credible dispute found. The scite tally is 297 classified citation statements out of 384 citing publications: 19 supporting, 1 contradicting, 270 mentioning, 7 unclassified. I could not open the single contrasting statement. Scans of OpenAlex citing works from 2021 to 2026 turned up no re-analysis or critique of the pooled g. Independent meta-analyses agree. Sotola & Crede 2021 (Educ Psychol Rev; ERIC abstract) found d = 0.42 across 52 real-class samples (N = 7,864). Bangert-Drowns et al. 1991 (ERIC abstract) found about 0.5 SD for students who took at least one test versus none. Adesope et al. 2017 (abstract only, no numbers) found practice tests beat restudy and all other comparison conditions. (4) Currency is fine. The paper is from 2021 and no superseding classroom pooled estimate turned up. It is still cited as the reference classroom estimate in 2023 to 2026 papers. (5) It is not marketing. The source is a peer-reviewed APA journal. The claim's own scope note is correct: the abstract says nothing about video, Indian students, board exams, or sealed/timed papers. A 2024 study of nine STEM courses (Bego et al.) found significant spaced-retrieval effects in only 2 of the 9 courses. A 2026 Prolific experiment found no testing effect. A 2026 high-stakes study (Hao, Baird, El Masri) found d above 0.57 for testing versus restudy, but no testing advantage in a low-stakes sample (n=115). Limits: the full text is paywalled, so I did not check the paper's own publication-bias analysis. votes.evidence:
The claim matches its source and I could not refute it.

1. Source check. I fetched the cited HKBU page directly. Its text reads: "The current review integrated 48,478 students' data, extracted from 222 independent studies" and "overall testing (quizzing) raises student academic achievement to a medium extent (g = 0.499)". Its metadata gives Psychological Bulletin, vol 147, issue 4, pp 399-435, 2021/04, DOI 10.1037/bul0000309. Every number in the claim matches.

2. Independent indexes agree.
- PubMed (PMID 33683913) carries the same abstract. It is typed Meta-Analysis and Review, with no erratum or comment links.
- Crossref and OpenAlex give the same bibliographic data and abstract. OpenAlex marks it not retracted. Crossref has no update-to or updated-by entries.
- Europe PMC shows no comment or correction list.
- Semantic Scholar counts about 298 citing papers.

3. Scope note is accurate. The abstract names these moderators: control-condition learning strategy, test-format consistency, material matching, corrective feedback, number of test repetitions, test location and timepoint, treatment duration, and experimental design. It says nothing about video lessons, Indian students, board exams, or sealed or timed full-length papers.

4. Later literature restates the figure.
- A 2025 health-professions review (PMC12292765) says "a medium effect size in applied classroom settings (g = 0.50; Yang et al., 2021)".
- A 2024 paper (PMC10950551) says quizzing "enhanced learning by half a standard deviation (Hedges' g = 0.50)" and notes considerable heterogeneity.
- A 2023 Cognitive Research review (PMC10409703) cites Yang et al. as Evidence Level 1 (a meta-analysis).

5. Contradiction search. WebSearch was out of budget, so I used scholarly APIs instead. I scanned the abstracts of all 298 citing papers and mined the full text of 36 open-access citing papers via Europe PMC. None disputed g = 0.499, and none paired Yang et al. with publication-bias or overestimation language.

6. Qualifications, not refutations.
- A 2023 Frontiers in Psychology paper (PMC10783554) says Yang et al. found "virtually no advantage (Hedges' g = 0.095)" of retrieval practice over elaborative strategies such as concept mapping. So 0.499 is an average over mixed controls, mostly passive or restudy. It does not mean testing beats every other study method by half a standard deviation.
- Heterogeneity is high.
- Some real-course studies are weaker. A 2024 spaced-retrieval study across nine STEM courses found significant effects in only two.

7. Limits of my check.
- The full text is paywalled, so I could not read the body's confidence interval or publication-bias adjustments. I am relying on the authors' own abstract.
- I could not read the two 2025 Educational Psychology Review meta-analyses on retrieval practice versus elaborative encoding and on mathematics. Springer served a bot-challenge page and I did not bypass it. Nothing found suggests they supersede the 2021 estimate.

The source is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis in a top review journal. At about 5.5 years old it is still the benchmark classroom estimate. The claim is a faithful, non-cherry-picked reading of the abstract, and its scope note correctly bars extrapolation to ExamLeaf's contexts.

The claim is accurate and I could not refute it. I checked it against six independent records.

1) Cited source. I pulled the raw HTML of the HKBU Scholars page. It contains verbatim "integrated 48,478 students' data, extracted from 222 independent studies" and "overall testing (quizzing) raises student academic achievement to a medium extent (g = 0.499)". It also lists Psychological Bulletin, vol 147, issue 4, pp 399-435, Apr 2021, "Journal article > peer-review". The HKBU page is an institutional-repository mirror of a peer-reviewed APA article, so the "primary" label is loose but the content is faithful.

2) Independent indexes.
- The Europe PMC and PubMed abstract (PMID 33683913, PsycInfo record) is word-for-word identical.
- Crossref (DOI 10.1037/bul0000309, publisher APA) confirms 147(4):399-435.
- Crossref has no update-to or updated-by field. PubMed XML has no ErratumIn, RetractionIn or CommentIn. OpenAlex has is_retracted=false. A Crossref search found no "Correction to Yang et al." in Psychological Bulletin for 2021-2023.
- Citation counts are 290 (Crossref), 298 (Semantic Scholar) and 344 (OpenAlex). A 2025 Teaching of Psychology paper still cites "g = 0.499".

3) Full text. I read the author manuscript from the UAM repository (hdl.handle.net/10486/725400).
- The pooled g is 0.499 [0.442, 0.556] from a multilevel random-effects model over 574 effects.
- Heterogeneity is substantial: Q(573) = 4,822.
- 82.9% of effects are positive, 15.5% negative and 1.6% null.
- Five publication-bias checks found nothing noteworthy: p-curve, publication status, PET-PEESE (corrected g = 0.476 [0.330, 0.621]), trim-and-fill (0 missing) and 3PSM.
- The submitted version says 223 studies and 48,582 students. The published abstract and the claim say 222 and 48,478. That is a revision-stage difference, not a mismatch with the cited source.

4) Scope note. The abstract mentions no video lessons, Indian students, board exams or sealed/timed full papers, so the note is correct. The review included only classroom studies and excluded laboratory and online-distance studies.

Qualifications, none of which contradict the claim:
- Within-subjects g = 0.673 versus between-subjects 0.415.
- Against a restudy control g = 0.329, against no/filler activity 0.610.
- Out-of-class quizzes 0.401 versus in-class 0.514.
- No corrective feedback 0.374 versus feedback 0.537.
- Untested material 0.322.
- Elementary school 0.339; high school 0.653.
- Random assignment was not an inclusion criterion.
- The authors themselves note that large education RCTs average about 0.06 (Lortie-Forgues & Inglis 2019).

I found no published comment, rebuttal or superseding classroom-quizzing meta-analysis among the 298 citing papers I scanned. Three related papers do not touch the claim:
- Gereau & Mulligan 2026 (JEP:LMC) is about lab free-recall direct versus forward testing effects.
- A 2026 Frontiers in Psychology null result uses an online Prolific sample.
- A 2024 Int J STEM Educ study is about spacing, not testing versus no testing.

Limit: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so the contradiction search used Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar APIs. OpenAlex search was rate-limited.

claim: Guo, Kim and Rubin (2014) analysed 6,902,358 video-watching sessions (862 videos, 127,839 students) from four Fall 2012 edX math/science courses. Median engagement time (watch time per session, 1x-speed sessions) was at most 6 minutes whatever the video length, and students often got less than halfway through videos longer than 9 minutes. The shortest videos (0-3 min) had the highest engagement (75% of sessions lasted over three quarters of the video). Length was the strongest single predictor of engagement. This directly challenges a roughly 15-minute-per-chapter format, though the metric is engagement, not learning.
quote: "median engagement time is at most 6 minutes, regardless of total video length" (Guo, Kim & Rubin 2014, section 'Shorter Videos Are More Engaging')
publishDate: 2014-03-04 (L@S 2014, held 4-5 March 2014, Atlanta; ACM DOI 10.1145/2556325.2566239; data from Fall 2012 edX courses)

votes.evidence:
The claim survives. I read the primary PDF at the cited URL (ACM L@S 2014 camera-ready, 10 pages) and checked each element.

1. Table 2 ("Overview of the Fall 2012 edX courses") totals: 862 videos, 127,839 students, 6,902,358 watching sessions. The four courses are 6.00x (MIT intro CS), PH207x (Harvard statistics for public health), CS188.1x (Berkeley AI) and 3.091x (MIT solid-state chemistry). The text says all Fall 2012 courses were math/science-focused.

2. Section "Shorter Videos Are More Engaging" calls length by far the most significant indicator of engagement. Figure 2 uses five length buckets and 1x-speed sessions only (footnote: 76% of all sessions). It says median engagement is at most 6 min regardless of length. It says students often get less than halfway through videos over 9 min. It says 0-3 min videos had the highest engagement and the least variance, with 75% of sessions lasting over three quarters of the video. Every number in the claim matches.

3. Figure 2 medians, read from the plot: about 1.0, 4.2, 6.1, 5.6 and 3.2 min for the 0-3, 3-6, 6-9, 9-12 and 12-40 min buckets. Normalised, they are about 1.0, 1.0, 0.95, 0.55 and 0.19. A 15-min video therefore sits in the worst bucket, with about 3 min median watch time per session (about 19% of the video).

4. The paper itself addresses the 15-min format. Producers urge chunks under 6 min, and the authors note that "even a 15-minute chunk seems short" to instructors.

5. The "engagement, not learning" caveat matches the paper's Limitations section. It says the study is retrospective, not a controlled experiment. It says first-batch edX users were self-motivated early adopters who may not be representative. It says no conclusions about learning should be drawn from engagement alone.

6. Source quality: a peer-reviewed primary source with about 2,100 citations (Semantic Scholar 2,123; Crossref 1,306).

Minor nits, none fatal:
- "Predictor" is loose. The paper uses boxplots and Mann-Whitney tests, not a regression.
- The plot shows the 6-9 min median at about 6.1-6.2, against "at most 6" in the text.
- 127,839 is a sum of per-course counts, so a student in two courses counts twice.

Contradiction search: WebSearch quota was exhausted (200/200). I used the Semantic Scholar list of 2,123 citing papers and read two primary PDFs. Nothing disputes the numbers; later work only qualifies how far they generalise.
- Lagerstrom, Johanes and Ponsukcharoen (Stanford, ASEE 2015) say the "six-minute rule" is a myth not because it is false but because it should not harden into a universal law. In for-credit Stanford CS courses with 50-75 min videos, median session watch time was 12.1 min (13,107 sessions) and 13.0 min (17,034 sessions), about 4x Guo's. Once sessions were stitched together, most students watched 90-100% of each video. So Guo's per-session metric understates cumulative viewing in committed audiences.
- Geri, Winer and Zaks (Open University of Israel, 2017; 59 videos of 4-24 min; preliminary, single institution, aggregate data): for videos of 11 min or more, mean view time rose from 8.87 to 10.81 min and completion from 59.1% to 72.5% after embedded questions were added.
- Technology, Knowledge and Learning 2024 (doi 10.1007/s10758-024-09745-2, N=22): segmented videos gave higher learning gains, and the authors conclude length is not crucial for learning when meaningful segments are provided.
- The direction of the finding is corroborated by Humanit Soc Sci Commun 2022 (short videos gave +24.7% viewing time and +9.0% final exam score), SAGE Open 2022 (under 5 min beat 10-20 min, which beat over 30 min) and Med Educ Online 2025 (under 5 min gave higher retention).

Bottom line: the factual statements are accurate and well sourced. "Directly challenges the 15-minute format" is a fair but not conclusive inference. It rests on low-stakes, voluntary adult MOOC viewers in 2012 and on per-session data, so the effect for exam-motivated Class 12 students is unproven. Chaptered 15-min videos with embedded questions are a plausible mitigation.
