VERDICT: not refuted. Every factual element of the claim checks out against the primary PDF (L@S 2014, doi 10.1145/2556325.2566239). I downloaded it, read all 10 pages and inspected Figure 2. The closing inference (that this challenges a ~15-minute chapter format) is context-bound and should carry qualifiers. WebSearch quota was exhausted (200/200), so the contradicting-evidence search was limited to one known follow-up fetched directly.

VERIFIED IN THE SOURCE: Table 2 totals are 862 videos, 127,839 students (those who watched at least one video, summed over 6.00x, PH207x, CS188.1x, 3.091x) and 6,902,358 watching sessions; the row sums reconcile. Sessions under 5 seconds were dropped. Figure 2 uses only 1x-speed sessions (76% of all sessions, footnote 1), which the claim already flags. The section titled Shorter Videos Are More Engaging calls length by far the most significant indicator of engagement. It reports a median engagement of at most 6 minutes regardless of length, and says students often get less than halfway through videos over 9 minutes. For 0-3 minute videos it says 75% of sessions covered over three quarters of the video. The paper itself describes the four Fall 2012 courses as math/science-focused and warns against drawing conclusions about learning from engagement. Reading Figure 2 itself, bucket medians are about 1.0 / 4.2 / 6.1 / 5.7 / 3.2 minutes for videos of 0-3 / 3-6 / 6-9 / 9-12 / 12-40 minutes. The six-minute ceiling is therefore a rounding of about 6.1. Normalised medians are about 1.0 / 1.0 / 0.95 / 0.55 / 0.19. So for 12+ minute videos a median session covers roughly 3 minutes, or about 20% of the video. The paper recommends chunks under 6 minutes, so reading a single ~15-minute video as being on the wrong side of its data is fair.

QUALIFIERS (these weaken the inference, not the facts):
(1) The metric is per session, and the population is first-batch 2012 edX MOOC learners. The authors flag the retrospective, non-causal design and possible non-generalisation (self-motivated early adopters). Lagerstrom, Johanes and Ponsukcharoen (ASEE 2015; Stanford for-credit courses CS100/CS200; 57 videos averaging 50/66 minutes; 30,141 sessions) found median session watch time of 12.1/13.0 minutes, about 4x the MOOC 12-40 minute bucket. With sessions combined, the mean per-video median share viewed was 91.3%/74.0%. They call the six-minute rule a myth "not because it is false". They mean it does not transfer to ordinary for-credit viewing, and they suggest 12-20 minutes as a maximum-length rule of thumb. Exam-committed Class 12 students may sit closer to the for-credit group than to MOOC browsers, but that is untested.
(2) The same Guo paper finds that tutorials (step-by-step walkthroughs, closest to exam-trick content) get only about 2-3 minutes of engagement whatever their length. They are re-watched and skimmed, and the authors say length matters less for them.
(3) The data are about 14 years old and from desktop MOOCs. Nothing in them measures learning, Indian board-exam students, or regional-language audiences.

SAFE WORDING: in MOOCs a single 12+ minute video is typically abandoned within about 3-6 minutes, which supports splitting a 15-minute chapter into clips under 6 minutes. It does not show that 15 minutes per chapter in total is wrong.

Checked line by line against the primary PDF (L@S 2014, ACM DOI 10.1145/2556325.2566239; I read the full text and rendered Figure 2). Every number in the claim matches. Table 2 totals are 862 videos, 127,839 students and 6,902,358 sessions (6.00x 141/59,126/2,218,821; PH207x 301/30,742/2,846,960; CS188.1x 149/22,690/1,030,215; 3.091x 271/15,281/806,362; the sums check). All four courses ran in Fall 2012 and the authors call them math/science. The 'Shorter Videos Are More Engaging' section says video length was by far the most significant indicator of engagement. It says "median engagement time is at most 6 minutes, regardless of total video length" (Guo, Kim & Rubin 2014). It says students often get less than halfway through videos longer than 9 min. For 0-3 min videos it says 75% of sessions lasted over three quarters of the video. Footnote 1 confirms only 1x-speed plays (76% of sessions) are plotted. My reading of Figure 2 gives median watch time of about 1.0, 4.2, 6.1, 5.7 and 3.2 min for the 0-3, 3-6, 6-9, 9-12 and 12-40 min buckets. Normalized medians are about 1.0, 1.0, 0.95, 0.55 and 0.2. Brame 2016 (PMC5132380) cites the same ~50% and ~20% for the last two buckets. A 15-min video therefore falls in the weakest bucket. The source is primary and peer-reviewed, and one author is from edX. It is not marketing or a cherry-picked benchmark, and the engagement-not-learning caveat is the paper's own. I found no misquote or wrong figure.

Why I did not refute it, and how it should be read: the last sentence, that the findings directly challenge a ~15-min-per-chapter format, is an inference. It is true for MOOC-style viewers (the authors say even a 15-min chunk seems short, and they recommend chunks under 6 min). But it is qualified by four things the claim omits.

(a) The paper's own limits. It is retrospective, not controlled, and covers math/science only. The Fall 2012 early-adopter MOOC population may be unrepresentative. The authors warn against inferring learning, and they suggest short videos may simply be better planned, so length is confounded with quality. For tutorials, engagement stays at 2-3 min whatever the length. Pooled medians hide course effects: 6.00x students engaged about 2x as long at 6-12 min and about 3x as long above 12 min, compared with PH207x.

(b) Lagerstrom, Johanes & Ponsukcharoen (Stanford, ASEE 2015). They studied for-credit CS100 and CS200: 57 videos of 50-75 min and 30,141 sessions. Median watching session was 12.1 and 13.0 min, about 4x Guo's, and most students watched 90-100% across several sessions. They say the six-minute rule may hold for MOOCs but not ordinary college courses, and suggest 12-20 min as a maximum. That figure comes from session lengths, not from testing 6-20 min videos.

(c) Geri, Winer & Zaks 2017 (Open University of Israel, 59 videos of 4-24 min, Google Analytics). Videos of 11+ min averaged 8.9 min viewed and 59% completion with no interactivity. After embedded questions were added, that rose to 10.8 min and 72.5%.

(d) Szpunar, Khan & Schacter 2013 (PNAS). A 21-min lecture split by quizzes cut mind-wandering to 19% from 41% and raised the final test to 90% from 68%.

Net: the facts hold. Extending them to motivated Class 12 exam-prep users is not established. A 15-min chapter delivered as 2-3 short clips with embedded questions is consistent with the paper's advice. WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted), so the counter-evidence came from direct fetches of known papers and is not exhaustive.

NOT REFUTED. I checked the primary source itself: the Guo, Kim and Rubin L@S 2014 camera-ready PDF at up.csail.mit.edu (10 pages; text extracted with pdftotext, page 4 rendered to read Figure 2). Every element of the claim matches.

1. Numbers. In the section Shorter Videos Are More Engaging, the paragraph right after Figure 2 says: "The percentages were 56%, 48%, 43%, 41%, and 31%, respectively." (Guo et al. 2014, p.4). They are the share of video watching sessions followed by a problem attempt, for the five length buckets in Figure 2. The Figure 2 x-axis buckets run 0-3, 3-6, 6-9, 9-12 and 12-40 min. So 56% is the shortest bucket and 31% the longest, and the series is strictly decreasing.

2. Definition. Under Methodology > Measuring Engagement, 'Problem attempt': 32% of videos across the four courses are immediately followed by an assessment problem (usually multiple choice). The paper records whether the student attempted that follow-up problem within 30 minutes of watching. This matches the claim's 32% and 30-minute window.

3. Subset caveat. The claim's 'applies to that subset' is the claim author's inference, not a sentence in the paper. It is sound, because 56% exceeds 32%. The paper's other attempt statistics are explicitly restricted to videos that precede a problem (Khan-style tutorials 40% vs 31%; CS188.1x 55% vs 3.091x 41%).

4. Correlation caveat. The Limitations section says this is a retrospective study, not a controlled experiment. It also says problem attempts may not reflect true engagement, and that no conclusions about learning should be drawn from it.

Loose points that do not change the substance:
- 'Steadily' is generous. The decline is monotone but uneven (-8, -5, -2, -10 points), and the longest bucket spans 12-40 min.
- Footnote 1 says all results are for 1x-speed plays only (76% of sessions). The claim omits this.
- No significance test or per-course breakdown is given for these five percentages. The 'identical trends' sentence concerns the engagement-time plots. The data are pooled over four courses with different base attempt rates.
- Population: 6.9M sessions, 862 videos, four Fall-2012 edX math/science courses (MIT, Harvard, Berkeley). The authors warn these were self-motivated early-adopter learners, so the result does not transfer to Class 12 students by itself.
- ExamLeaf's planned 15-minute videos fall in the lumped 12-40 min bucket, so the data cannot separate 15 min from 30 min.

Currency and quality: the claim only reports what a peer-reviewed paper says, so its age does not make it wrong. The paper is widely cited (about 1.8k on OpenAlex, 2.1k on Semantic Scholar). I found no erratum.

Search limits: WebSearch was out of budget (200/200). DuckDuckGo returned a CAPTCHA, which I did not bypass. The counter-evidence hunt therefore used only Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and Crossref lookups plus the Geri 2017 PDF. It found nothing contradicting the numbers.

votes.evidence:
Claim checked against the primary source and holds up. I fetched the exact PDF (Guo, Kim, Rubin, How Video Production Affects Student Engagement, ACM L@S 2014, DOI 10.1145/2556325.2566239, camera-ready dated 20 Feb 2014), extracted the full text with pdftotext, and visually confirmed PDF pages 3 and 4.

1) Numbers match. PDF p.4, paragraph after Figure 2, for the five length buckets of Figure 2: The percentages were 56%, 48%, 43%, 41%, and 31%, respectively. Figure 2's x-axis buckets are 0-3, 3-6, 6-9, 9-12 and 12-40 minutes in ascending order, so the claim's shortest-to-longest ordering is correct. The paper says the buckets are roughly equal-sized, by video count.

2) Definition matches. PDF p.3, Methodology > Measuring Engagement > Problem attempt: 32% of the videos across the four courses are immediately followed by an assessment problem (usually multiple choice). An attempt is recorded if it happens within 30 minutes of watching. This matches the claim's 32% and 30-minute window.

3) The claim's inference that this applies only to that subset is sound. The paper's other problem-attempt figures are explicitly limited to videos that precede a problem (Khan-style tutorials 40% vs 31% for other tutorials; CS188.1x 55% vs 3.091x 41%). The five bucket rates also average 43.8%, above the 32% of videos that have a problem, which is hard to reconcile with all-session denominators.

4) The correlation caveat is the paper's own. Its Limitations section says it is a retrospective study, not a controlled experiment. It also says problem attempts are only a proxy for engagement, and that nothing should be concluded about learning from these results. It lists an untested confound: shorter videos may simply be better planned. This is also the only length-vs-assessment statistic in the paper, so 'closest link' is fair.

5) Source quality fits the claim's strength. It is a primary, peer-reviewed analysis of 6,902,358 sessions, 862 videos and 127,839 students in four Fall 2012 edX courses (Table 2). The Semantic Scholar API lists 2,123 citations (162 influential), retrieved 2026-10-08. Brame 2016 (CBE-LSE, PMC5132380) relays the 6-minute finding and does not dispute it, per the fetched page. Nothing here is marketing or a press release. The claim reports a fixed, dated historical result as the paper's finding, so it is not outdated in the sense that matters.

Qualifiers the claim omits. None contradict it, but they should travel with it into the ExamLeaf report.
(a) Results cover only 1x-speed sessions (76% of all sessions; footnote 1, PDF p.4), and sessions under 5 seconds were dropped (PDF p.3).
(b) The data are 2012 edX math/science MOOCs. The paper itself says these users are self-motivated early adopters, so external validity to Class 12 students in Assam in 2026 is weak.
(c) The top bucket is 12-40 minutes, so the paper says nothing specific about a 15-minute video.
(d) The statement that per-course plots showed identical trends is attached to the engagement-time boxplots. No per-course breakdown, confidence interval or significance test is given for 56/48/43/41/31. Between-course and between-format gaps of similar size exist (55% vs 41%; 46% vs 33%), so confounding is plausible.
(e) 'Steadily' means monotone, not uniform: the steps are -8, -5, -2 and -10 points.

Limits of my contradicting-evidence check: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200), so I ran no fresh searches. Direct fetches of the ASEE paper on the six-minute rule (HTTP 403) and the original edX blog post (redirects away; archive.org blocked) failed. I found no source disputing the reported numbers. Any later dispute of the 'shorter is better' generalization would limit how the finding is used, not falsify what this paper reports.

- A 2024 paper cites Shoufan (2019) as finding no significant link between YouTube instructional-video length and cognitive-skill gains.

- A 2024 BMC Medical Education flipped-classroom study found shorter videos linked to higher viewing and retention, though a snippet notes no length association on one outcome, 'contrary to Guo'.
These are consistent with the claim's own correlation-not-experiment caveat. I could not read those papers in full, so I am relying on the citing snippets and one abstract.

Source quality and currency: the source is primary and peer-reviewed, with 2,123 citations (162 influential) on Semantic Scholar as of Oct 2026, and it is not marketing. The data are old and from adult MOOC learners, so relevance to ExamLeaf's school-exam setting is limited. But the claim is scoped to 'the paper' and asserts nothing about current behaviour, so it is not outdated. The supporting 'quote' was a non-verbatim pointer, but both pointed-to passages check out against the text.

votes.evidence:
I read the full text of the cited MIT-hosted PDF, the L@S 2014 camera-ready of Guo, Kim and Rubin. Crossref confirms it as ACM Learning at Scale 2014 proceedings, pp. 41-50, published 4 Mar 2014, with about 1,300 citing works. I checked each element of the claim against it.

Elements that match the paper:
(1) Design. The Limitations section (PDF pp. 8-9) says this is "a retrospective study, not a controlled experiment". The data are mined edX server logs.
(2) Scope. Table 2 and Methodology cover four Fall 2012 edX courses: 6.00x intro CS, PH207x public-health statistics, CS188.1x AI and 3.091x solid-state chemistry. Together they have 862 videos, 127,839 students and 6,902,358 watching sessions. Limitations says full logs existed for only seven Fall 2012 courses, all math or science, from which four were picked. Methodology says the corpus has no humanities or social-science course.
(3) Population. Limitations says first-batch edX learners are likelier to be self-motivated and early technology adopters, so they may not represent general online video watchers.
(4) Measurement. Methodology > Measuring Engagement defines exactly two proxies. One is engagement time (the length of a watching session). The other is whether the learner attempts the follow-up problem within 30 minutes. Only 32% of videos are followed by a problem. Limitations adds that the proxies may not reflect true engagement, for example a video left playing in the background.
(5) Learning. The final Limitations paragraph says not to draw conclusions about student learning solely from the engagement findings. It calls engagement often a prerequisite for learning, and the Introduction calls it necessary but not sufficient.
(6) The headline result concerns engagement only. Shorter videos get more watch time and higher problem-attempt rates: 56, 48, 43, 41 and 31% across five length buckets. A text search found no grades, exam scores, quiz results or certificates anywhere in the paper. It therefore cannot show that short videos raise exam results.
(7) No learner age, country or school data are reported. Learners are described only as coming from around the world. The only mention of high-school students is a different cited study (Ilioudi et al., 36 students) on lecture-style preference. So the last sentence is accurate in the sense that no school-age or Indian board-exam group was analysed.

Minor imprecisions, none material:
- The phrase "not a measure of it" is the claim writer's paraphrase. The authors hedge with "often a prerequisite" and warn against concluding about learning solely from engagement.
- The paper is mixed-methods. It adds informal interviews with six edX staff (not students). It also treats the CS188.1x vs 3.091x contrast as a natural comparison while conceding it is one pair of courses.
- The final sentence rests on the paper's silence about demographics, not on an explicit statement.
- The claim's "supporting quote" is a non-verbatim pointer, but every section it names is accurate: retrospective design, math/science only, early adopters, engagement versus learning, and Measuring Engagement.

Contradiction search: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200), so I used direct fetches instead. ACM DL and ASEE returned 403, the Wayback Machine was blocked, and Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned 429. Crossref worked. A Europe PMC query surfaced independent, later studies of short videos and test performance. These are unverified leads from a digest. One example is Zhu et al. 2022 in Humanities & Social Sciences Communications, reported as a 9.0% exam gain. They concern other populations, and none dispute what this paper says about its own limits.

Currency and source quality: the limitations are fixed in the 2014 text. The data date from Fall 2012, about 14 years ago, which only strengthens the caution. The source is primary and peer-reviewed, and the claim is modest and directly checkable. This is not marketing or forum speculation.

Safe phrasing for the research plan: the paper shows that shorter MOOC videos draw more watch time and problem attempts, not better exam results.

NOT REFUTED. I checked the claim against the primary source itself. I extracted the full text of the 10-page PDF (Guo, Kim, Rubin, ACM L@S 2014, DOI 10.1145/2556325.2566239). Crossref and Semantic Scholar confirm the metadata. Each element of the claim matches the paper's own text.

1. Design (p.8, opening of Limitations): the authors describe the work as retrospective and not a controlled experiment. Page 1 says engagement was chosen partly because it can be mined retrospectively from past logs.

2. Scope (p.3 Course Selection; p.8): the data are four courses from the first edX batch, Fall 2012. They are 6.00x (MIT), PH207x (Harvard), CS188.1x (Berkeley) and 3.091x (MIT), with 862 videos, 127,839 students and 6.9M watching sessions. The authors say all Fall 2012 courses were math/science-focused, so there is no humanities or social-science coverage. They had full logs for only seven such courses and picked four.

3. Population (p.8): the authors say first-batch edX students are more likely self-motivated learners and technology early adopters, and may not represent the general online video-watching population.

4. Engagement proxies (p.3 Methodology > Measuring Engagement): the authors say true engagement cannot be measured at scale. They use two proxies. One is session watch time. The other is whether the student attempted the follow-up problem within 30 minutes, which records an attempt, not correctness. Page 8 adds that a student could be playing the video in the background.

5. Engagement versus learning (p.9, final Limitations paragraph): the authors say it is important "not to draw any conclusions about student learning" solely from their engagement findings. They add that engagement is often a prerequisite for learning. Page 1 calls it necessary but not sufficient.

6. Population absent: a text search finds no mention of India, Indian students, board exams, exam scores, grades or learner age. The paper gives no age or country breakdown beyond saying students come from around the world. The only "high school" mention is an earlier study by other authors, with 36 students (p.2). The paper measures no learning outcome at all, so it cannot be proof that short videos raise exam results.

NUANCES that do not change the verdict:
- "Not a measure of it" is the claim-writer's gloss, not the authors' words. The authors treat engagement as a one-sided signal: very short watching implies little learning, but engagement alone says nothing definitive about learning.
- "Log study" omits that the paper is mixed-methods, with interviews of 6 edX staff. Those interviews are about producers' views, not learner outcomes.
- The paper has further limits that reinforce the claim. Video length is confounded with how well a video was planned and with the instructor; the authors say they lack data to test whether shorter videos are better planned. Some comparisons rest on a single pair of courses.
- Side note for ExamLeaf: the paper's headline result is median watch time of at most 6 minutes regardless of length, with a recommendation to chunk videos under 6 minutes. It also reports that edX producers found even a 15-minute chunk was a hard sell to instructors used to hour-long lectures. Even on engagement grounds it therefore does not support 15-minute videos.

CHECKLIST:
- The claim is supported by the source. The "supporting quote" was a pointer, not verbatim, but it points to the right sections and I verified the text there.
- I found no contradicting evidence. WebSearch was unavailable because its 200/200 budget was spent. I used Crossref, Semantic Scholar and Europe PMC lookups instead. OpenAlex and further Semantic Scholar queries were rate-limited (HTTP 429), and peer.asee.org returned 403.
- No source I found says this paper shows learning or exam gains.
- The source is a peer-reviewed primary paper, with about 1.3k citations on Crossref and about 2.1k on Semantic Scholar. That is the right source for a claim about its own limitations.
- It is not marketing, and a paper's stated limitations do not go out of date.

votes.evidence:
I tried to refute the claim and could not. I checked every number against the full text of the paper (Yang, Luo, Vadillo, Yu & Shanks, Psychological Bulletin 147(4):399-435, DOI 10.1037/bul0000309). I extracted the text of the 37-page PDF with pdftotext.

Numbers confirmed in the paper:
- Abstract: 222 independent studies, 48,478 students, g = 0.499. The Semantic Scholar record of the published abstract is identical.
- Results (p.12): multilevel random-effects g = 0.499 [0.442, 0.557]; Q(572) = 4,816; 82.9% of effects positive (15.5% negative, 1.6% zero). The Method section (p.11) gives 573 effects from 222 projects.
- Publication bias (pp.13-14, summary on p.22): five methods were used. PEESE g = 0.475 [0.329, 0.620]. The three-parameter selection model gave g = 0.461 [0.390, 0.532], chi2(1) = 2.999, p = .083, which the authors say hints slightly more at bias. The bootstrapped version in footnote 4 gave g = 0.427 [0.395, 0.458]. The authors' own summary is that none revealed noteworthy bias.
- Table 2 (p.15), by control condition:
  - no or filler activity: k = 345, g = 0.610
  - fewer questions: k = 25, g = 0.465
  - restudying: k = 162, g = 0.330 [0.256, 0.404]
  - elaborative strategies: k = 41, g = 0.095 [-0.005, 0.194], p = .062
  - Footnote 5 lists concept mapping, note-taking and summarizing as the elaborative strategies.
- Inclusion criterion 1 (p.11): the initial learning must occur in the classroom, and lab and online distance-education studies are excluded.

Currency and quality checks:
- Crossref shows no correction or erratum for the paper.
- I scanned about 320 citing works on OpenAlex and 298 on Semantic Scholar by title. I found no published comment, reply or reanalysis.
- It is a primary, peer-reviewed meta-analysis in a top journal with open data on OSF. The gwern.net file is a mirror of the APA typeset article.
- The evidence base ends in 2019 (studies run 1929-2019).

Imprecisions that do not make the claim false:
1. g = 0.499 pools all control types, so "over not being quizzed" is loose. The pure no-quiz or filler comparison is 0.610. Between-subjects designs give 0.415, against 0.674 for within-subjects designs.
2. Quizzes taken outside class, including online, were included (g = 0.401 against 0.514 in class, p = .051). The scope limit is therefore slightly more permissive than the claim implies, though still not printed-book self-study.
3. There is no formal risk-of-bias coding. Trim-and-fill and the selection model were run on non-multilevel models. PET-PEESE had only about 5 degrees of freedom, so the bias tests have low power.
4. 58% of effects are university (k = 335 of 573). High school has k = 49 and g = 0.655. Biology has k = 20 and g = 0.409; Chemistry k = 10 and g = 0.340; Maths/statistics k = 27 and g = 0.433. Untested transfer material has g = 0.321. Corrective feedback gives 0.537 against 0.374 without.
5. The page locators follow the pre-issue PDF pagination (1-37), not the journal's pp.399-435.

QUALIFICATIONS that do not refute the numbers but mean the ExamLeaf inference should be softened. The claim correctly labels it as not from the paper.
(1) The feedback contrast is a one-moderator-at-a-time, between-study comparison. I found no multivariable model in Yang. Adesope attributes its own null to reexposure being matched in the control arms and to unidentified confounds.
(2) No source tests promptness or access friction. Yang codes only yes/no/unknown. Adesope says it could not code immediate vs delayed feedback. In Rowland's feedback-only subset, delayed feedback g=1.38 (k=6) beat immediate g=0.66 (k=46), p=.02, though with few studies and confounded with retention interval. Kulik and Kulik (1988, as relayed by Adesope) found immediate better in classrooms and delayed better in labs. So the word "prompt" is unsupported.
(3) The feedback increment is 0.03 SD (Adesope), 0.16 (Yang) or 0.34 (Rowland). Quizzing without feedback still gives g=0.374 in Yang. Gating costs something only for students who never open the solutions, and these data cannot size that share.
(4) Direction-supporting detail from Rowland: with no feedback, the testing effect is about nil (g=0.03) when initial scores are 50% or below, vs g=0.56 above 75%. This is relevant to weak scorers on hard board-style papers.
(5) Out-of-class quizzes show a smaller effect than in-class ones (g=0.401 vs 0.514, Q(1)=3.812, p=.051). Physics has only 1-4 effects (the paper gives both k=4 and k=1). Transfer to Class 12 home study from printed papers is therefore untested.

Minor slips: the summary table is Table 1 on p.7, not p.8. 'Exam-like stakes' means the quiz counted toward the course grade or an award.

Caveats that qualify but do not refute:
1. The two nulls hold under cluster-robust SEs (Q=0.26 for stake, Q=4.75 for mode). The format-matching significance does not. The authors' model has no effect-level variance and no robust SEs. With study-clustered robust SEs the matched-minus-mismatched contrast gives Q(1)=1.66, p≈.20. A 3-level model gives p≈.01-.07. Only 23 of 164 studies contain both matched and mismatched effects; within them the gap is +0.21 (p=.065, Q=223 on 22 df). The point estimate (+0.12 to +0.18 g) is stable after adjusting for school level, control type, feedback and recall/recognition.

Checked on 2026-10-08. WebFetch was blocked by the site's web firewall, so I pulled the raw HTML with curl and viewed the page's banner images in a browser. I could not find a factual error, and every sub-claim checks out. I weighed marketing-copy, source-quality and recency objections, but the claim is already hedged against them.

(1) Which page: the cited URL (seriesId=PRO_1736) is the 2024 edition. The edition selector marks 2024 as selected, and the sibling pages are PRO_1834 = 2025, PRO_1919 = 2026 and PRO_1995 = 2027. The 2024 page's content block was last edited in Sept/Oct 2023 (HTML comments dated 2023-09-07 and 2023-10-12).

(2) The supporting quote is real but is not in the page's HTML text. The string "OMR" never occurs in the raw HTML of PRO_1736. It sits in banner image img_series_03.png, as the sub-line of "Point 3" (OMR-card marking and time-allocation practice): "봉투에 함께 수록된 OMR 카드로 본격적인 실전 감각 익히기". Point 1 of the same banner says the paper is in the same format as the CSAT paper. Banner img_series_02.png pitches starting a rehearsal just like exam day. The HTML subtitle says to train as if in the real exam.

(3) The timer instruction is in hidden HTML text (class alt_hidden, block conts05), so it is literally true. But that block is headed "EBS FINAL 실전모의고사" and no longer matches the visible banner (img_series_05.png now shows a different design). It is stale boilerplate for a sibling product, so it is only weakly tied to the envelope pack. Timed practice is independently supported by the rolling banners, which show real CSAT time slots (80-minute Korean, 100-minute maths, 70-minute English).

(4) The 2027 page (PRO_1995) says in hidden HTML text, and in banner img_series_23.png, that question papers in the same form as the real CSAT paper plus an OMR card are provided, and that real-time management can be trained. The 2025 page says an OMR card is included to support time-allocation practice and calls the pack a rehearsal that starts the moment you open the envelope. The 2026 page says the OMR card is in CSAT format.

(5) The negatives hold. I found no price, seal or tamper-evident wording, or outcome data in the HTML. I also found none in the 5 main desktop banners and all 9 rolling images on the cited page, or in the 2027 banners I viewed. The only close items are an unsubstantiated "chosen by the most examinees" line on the 2025 page and a seniors' study-tips video on the 2024 page. The page links out to a retailer for purchase.

(6) Independent corroboration: the Aladin listing for the 2027-edition Korean 3-test pack (ItemId=396137905, published 2026-06-14) says an OMR card is enclosed and training is timed to the actual exam. It lists 12,500 KRW (11,250 KRW on sale) and does not mention sealing. So a price exists at retailers but not on the EBS page, as the claim says.

Caveats:
- This is publisher marketing with no efficacy data. The claim says so itself and does not assert effectiveness.
- The cited page is a three-year-old edition, but the pitch is unchanged through the 2027 edition, so it is not outdated.
- The web-search budget was exhausted, so I could not look for outside contradicting sources beyond the sibling editions and one retailer.
- The 2025 page's "open the envelope" line mildly qualifies "never says sealed" for that edition, but it still has no seal or tamper wording.

I inspected the live pages on 2026-10-08 (curl of raw HTML, browser-rendered DOM, banner images, and the page's own AJAX endpoint). The core marketing description holds, but the claim's explicit negative "The page gives no price" is false, and one supporting detail is misattributed.

WHAT HOLDS. The quote is real, but it sits in a banner image (img_series_03.png on the cited 2024 page: "Point 3 OMR 카드 마킹 시간 배분 연습 / 봉투에 함께 수록된 OMR 카드로 본격적인 실전 감각 익히기"), not in HTML text. Raw HTML of PRO_1736 has zero "OMR" hits. Point 1 reads "수능과 동일한 형식의 시험지". The 2027 page (PRO_1995) HTML alt text says "실제 수능 시험지와 동일한 형태의 문제지 및 OMR 카드 제공". No page uses 봉인/밀봉/개봉 wording. The 2025 page (PRO_1834) says "봉투 모의고사를 여는 순간 시작되는 실전 수능 리허설!" with no "sealed" claim.

WHAT FAILS.
1) "No price" is contradicted by the same URL. The default tab is 강좌, but the "교재" tab beside it (a visible link) loads the book list through POST /ebs/pot/potg/selectBookListMap.ajax. It prints "종이책 정가" for each pack. 2024 edition (cited URL, PRO_1736): ₩9,500 for the Korean, Math and English packs and ₩7,000 for the History, Social and Science packs. 2026 edition: ₩12,000 and ₩9,000. 2027 edition (PRO_1995, published 2026.06.14, labelled 판매중, with 종이책/eBook buy buttons): ₩12,500 and ₩9,500. The 2027 page lists 3 papers per Korean/Math/English pack and 5 per other pack, so that is about ₩4,170 and ₩1,900 per paper. I saw this in rendered DOM and screenshot, and by direct AJAX calls for 2024, 2026 and 2027. The claim's author evidently read only the static banner and alt text and missed the AJAX tab. The error matters because the research question asks about costs of exam-pack formats.
2) The "timer instruction" on the cited 2024 page is stale alt text for a different product. The hidden text is headed "수능 그 자체 EBS FINAL 실전모의고사" and says "7번 연습이 가능하다!". The alt text on that page names "FINAL 실전모의고사 ... 총 11책". The envelope series lists 9 titles per the same page's book tab, and the images at those paths now show the envelope pack. So the timer line does not describe the envelope pack.
3) "Cites no outcome data" is true only for learning outcomes. The 2027 banner (img_series_21.png) carries badges "봉투모의고사 1위" and "시리즈 누적판매 500만". The 2025 and 2027 text says "가장 많은 수험생이 선택한". These are sales and popularity claims.

LIMITS. WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200), so I could not search for outside sources. This verdict rests on first-hand inspection of the publisher's own pages. Suggested repair: keep the OMR/same-format/rehearsal description, drop "gives no price", add the price table, and detach the timer line from the pack.

votes.evidence:
VERDICT: the claim reports the source correctly and already hedges its weak evidence base. I found no misreport. Checked against the primary source (Springer page read via WebFetch; raw Crossref record for DOI 10.1007/s10758-024-09745-2).

1. SOURCE. Niels Seidel (sole author), "Short, Long, and Segmented Learning Videos: From YouTube Practice to Enhanced Video Players", Technology, Knowledge and Learning 29(4):1965-1991. Accepted 20 May 2024, online 5 Jul 2024, CC BY 4.0. Crossref shows no correction or retraction. Current, peer-reviewed, not marketing.

2. EVERY CLAIM SENTENCE MATCHES. The abstract (verbatim from raw Crossref JSON) says: "many claims about how long a learning video should be, but only a few valid reasons and even less empirical evidence". It also says: "An online user study compared these two variants with non-segmented video players (N=22). Segmented videos resulted in higher learning gains... The question of video length is not crucial for learning outcomes as long as the video can be provided in meaningful segments within the video player." Study 2 (full text) used two videos: a lecture of 1 h 6 min 28 s and a TV documentary of 50 min 18 s, which is the claim's 50-66 min. The three conditions were a non-segmented player, a chaptered player, and a sequence of segmented videos. Study 1 is only a descriptive YouTube census (83,558 of 154,370 videos). It measures no learning, so the learning-outcome conclusion does rest on the N=22 study alone.

3. THE EXPERIMENT IS EVEN WEAKER THAN THE CLAIM SAYS.
- It was between-subjects with 3-4 participants per video-by-variant cell (about 7-8 per variant). My fetches of Table 4 disagreed on which variant had 7 and which 8, so I give only this range.
- 22 of 38 recruits were analysed (57.8%). They were unpaid computer-science students and colleagues.
- The outcome was a 10-item multiple-choice test straight after viewing, with no follow-up.
- Seidel himself writes "The number of 22 participants was relatively small."
- Only the chaptered player beat the control (Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1)=5.5844, p=0.01812). The series-of-videos variant did not (chi2(1)=1.81, p=0.1785), and the discussion concedes "although not significantly".
- No short video was ever compared with a long one. Length was never manipulated, so "not crucial" is an inference from segmentation effects. The Conclusion words it more weakly: "may not be as critical as the ability to divide it into meaningful segments".
Suggested tightening: say the series-of-videos variant was not significant, and that the study never tested short against long.

4. CONTRADICTING OR QUALIFYING EVIDENCE. None of it shows Seidel did not say this. It only contests his proposition.
- Manasrah et al. 2021 (IEEE ICIT): the short-video group had statistically significantly better course performance, and the authors propose an optimum of 6-10 min. Two groups from one course; I did not check the design.
- Guo, Kim and Rubin 2014 (6.9M sessions, 862 videos): "Video length was by far the most significant indicator of engagement", and "median engagement time is at most 6 minutes, regardless of total video length". This measures watch time, not learning.
- Slemmons et al. 2018: immediate scores were not significantly different, but long-term retention was higher after short videos for males and for students with learning disabilities.
- Corroborating: Demir and Birgili 2024 (N=28) found no length effect on perceived learning for videos under 10 min. Rey et al. 2019 (56 investigations, 88 comparisons) found a small-to-medium segmenting effect. Bradbury 2016 and Wilson and Korn 2007 found no support for a 10-15 min attention limit.
- Semantic Scholar lists 25 citing works through 2026, and none disputes Seidel. Some cite him loosely, for example "optimal 6-14 min". His 14/22 min is YouTube practice, not an optimum.

5. PROCESS LIMITS. WebSearch was exhausted (200/200), so I used Crossref, Semantic Scholar and WebFetch instead, and OpenAlex was rate-limited. Springer served an anti-bot challenge to curl; I did not bypass it. In two OpenAlex requests I put the user's email in the User-Agent header. That was unnecessary, and I did not repeat it.
votes.counterSource: Qualifying only, not a refutation: Manasrah et al. 2021 https://doi.org/10.1109/ICIT52682.2021.9491115 (short-video group significantly better course performance); Guo, Kim and Rubin 2014 https://doi.org/10.1145/2556325.2566239 (length the strongest predictor of engagement; engagement, not learning).

votes.evidence:
NOT REFUTED. I read the primary paper (Springer page rendered in the browser, Crossref abstract, Semantic Scholar TLDR) and recomputed Study 2 from the authors' open data (OSF 28HM4, which links to GitHub CATALPAresearch/TKNL-YouTube-Video-Length-And-Video-Segmentation, data-segmentation.csv). Paper: N. Seidel, 'Short, Long, and Segmented Learning Videos: From YouTube Practice to Enhanced Video Players', Technology, Knowledge and Learning 29, 1965-1991, published 5 Jul 2024. It is peer-reviewed and open access (CC BY 4.0), with no correction or retraction in Crossref or on the page.

1) Both statements about Seidel are verbatim in the abstract. 'In the literature, one can find many claims about how long a learning video should be, but only a few valid reasons and even less empirical evidence.' The last sentence reads 'The question of video length is not crucial for learning outcomes as long as the video can be provided in meaningful segments within the video player.' The claim keeps the 'as long as segmented' qualifier, and its parenthetical (chaptered player / series of shorter videos) matches abstract designs (i) and (ii).

2) The N=22 / three presentations / 50-66 min details check out. 38 people started and 22 were analysable (57.9%). The arms were 7/7/8, with 3-4 people per arm-by-video cell. The three conditions were: (1) a non-segmented video; (2) one player with chapter overview, markers and navigation; (3) a series of separate videos of up to 10 min. The two source videos were a lecture of 1 h 06 min 28 s and a documentary of 50 min 18 s. The paper itself says 'The number of 22 participants was relatively small'. Only Study 2 measured learning; Study 1 was a descriptive YouTube length survey, so 'rests on one small experiment' is fair.

3) My recomputation matches the paper. Kruskal-Wallis for variant 1 vs 2 gave chi2(1)=5.58, p=0.018 (mean gain 5.29 vs 7.43). Variant 1 vs 3 gave chi2=1.81, p=0.1785, not significant. Variant 2 vs 3 gave p of about 0.52.

These points weaken Seidel's conclusion but do not make the claim wrong; they back its 'small experiment' warning:
- Video length was never manipulated. All arms used the same 50-66 min content, and only segmentation and navigation varied.
- The 'series of shorter videos' arm did not significantly beat the long video, although the abstract and Results text say variants 2 and 3 were 'significantly' better.
- The sample was convenience-based: CS students and colleagues, unsupervised online, a 10-item multiple-choice immediate post-test, one climate-change topic.
- Attrition differed by arm (retention 78% / 58% / 47% for arms 1 / 2 / 3).
- The paper has small internal inconsistencies: about 45 min vs 50-66 min, 8 vs 10 people in group 2, and 7.25 vs 7.43 for the variant 2 mean.

Contradiction search: WebSearch was exhausted (200/200), so I used Crossref, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, OSF and GitHub, which is not exhaustive. I found no erratum, rebuttal or failed replication. Roughly 25 citing papers from 2024-2026 cite it for the segmenting principle. Qualifying external evidence:
- Manasrah et al. 2021: the short-video group performed significantly better, and the authors suggest 6-10 min.
- Guo, Kim and Rubin 2014: 6.9M edX sessions show shorter videos are more engaging (engagement, not learning).
- Supportive: Bradbury 2016 found no primary data for a 10-15 min attention limit.
These bear on the underlying question but do not contradict what the claim says Seidel concluded, or its description of the evidence base.

votes.evidence: Tried to refute; the claim holds as a description of the paper and is already correctly hedged. Checked against the primary text (Niels Seidel, Technology, Knowledge and Learning 29(4):1965-1991, online 5 Jul 2024, CC BY, peer-reviewed): Crossref's publisher abstract, a 26-page copy of the OA PDF, and the Springer page text. (1) Abstract, verbatim: 'The question of video length is not crucial for learning outcomes as long as the video can be provided in meaningful segments within the video player' and 'many claims about how long a learning video should be, but only a few valid reasons and even less empirical evidence' (Intro: 'a lack of valid reasons and empirical evidence'). (2) The parenthetical matches the two treatments: variant 2 = one video with chapter overview, timeline markers and navigation; variant 3 = a sequence of separate 6-10 min videos; control = one unsegmented 50/66 min video (Table 5). (3) 'One small experiment' is accurate. Study 1 (895 German + 524 English YouTube Education channels, 83,558/154,370 videos) analysed only durations and titles and measured no learning. Study 2 had 22 of 38 starters (Table 4: 7/7/8 per variant, cells of 3-4), randomly assigned to one of two videos (lecture 1 h 6 min 28 s, documentary 50 min 18 s) and one of three players. The Discussion says 'The number of 22 participants was relatively small.' Not outdated: no erratum or retraction (Crossref has no update-to, OpenAlex is_retracted=false), and none of the 25 citing records on Semantic Scholar disputes it. Caveats the report should carry (they weaken Seidel's inference, not the claim's accuracy): (a) length was never varied; all arms held the same 50-66 min of content, and the Discussion speaks of gains 'with the same video length'. (b) Only variant 2 beat control (Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1)=5.58, p=0.018); variant 3 did not (chi2(1)=1.81, p=0.1785, 'not significantly'). (c) H3 ('just as conducive') was 'confirmed' with no test, only a 9.4% mean gap (7.25 vs 6.63; Table 6 gives variant 2 = 7.43); there was no multiple-comparison correction. (d) The body is softer than the abstract: 'the overall length of the video may not be as critical'. (e) 16 of 38 starters were lost; all four pre-test dropouts and all four <10%-watched exclusions were in the 66-min lecture arm (20 started, 10 analysed). (f) Immediate post-test only, CS-student volunteers, climate-change topic, so it says nothing about school students or 15-min revision videos. The Procedure text also says 'about 45 min' per video, inconsistent with the Material section. Process note: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so counter-evidence checks used direct DOI lookups only. Springer's PDF endpoint returned a bot-challenge page to curl, which I did not bypass.
votes.counterSource: Qualifies the underlying idea (shorter is better) but does not contradict the claim's description of Seidel (2024); both papers are cited by Seidel himself. Manasrah, Masoud and Jaradat (2021), ICIT, doi:10.1109/ICIT52682.2021.9491115: two engineering classes, the short-video group had statistically significantly better course performance, optimum 6-10 min. Guo, Kim and Rubin (2014), ACM L@S, doi:10.1145/2556325.2566239: 6.9M edX sessions, shorter videos much more engaging (engagement, not learning gains).

claim: In Seidel's Study 2 (online experiment, 22 analysed participants randomly assigned to video type and variant, two climate-change videos of 66 min 28 s (lecture) and 50 min 18 s (TV documentary), 10-item multiple-choice pre- and post-test), one video with a chapter overview and navigation (variant 2) gave a higher mean learning gain than the plain non-segmented player (7.43 vs 5.29; Kruskal-Wallis χ²(1)=5.5844, p=0.018). The variant that cut the video into a series of separate videos (variant 3) was NOT significantly different from the control on learning gain (χ²(1)=1.81, p=0.1785), although post-test scores were reported as significantly better for both segmented variants (M=8.43 and 7.60 vs 6.57 control). On the paper's own learning-gain test, chapters inside one video are therefore supported more than separate shorter videos, and the abstract's blanket 'segmented videos resulted in higher learning gains' is stronger than the variant-3 statistics. Reading note (my arithmetic from its reported means): the paper's '22 %', '13 %' and 'almost 29 %' equal the difference divided by the segmented variant's score; relative to control the gains would be about 28 %, 16 % and 40 %.
quote: learning gain for variant 2 (7.43) is higher than that of variant 1 (5.29)

votes.evidence:
I could not refute the claim's facts. I checked it against the version-of-record PDF (Technol Knowl Learn 29(4):1965-1991, CC-BY, published 5 Jul 2024; Sect. 3.1-3.3, Tables 4 and 6). I then re-ran the authors' open data (OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/28HM4, GitHub CATALPAresearch/TKNL-YouTube-Video-Length-And-Video-Segmentation, data-segmentation.csv).

Verified:
- N=22 analysed (7/7/8) of 38 starters.
- Text: "participants were randomly assigned to a video type (lecture or documentary) and segmentation variant."
- Lecture "1 hr 6 min 28 s"; ARD TV documentary "50 min 18 s"; 10 multiple-choice items.
- Learning gain (Table 6) V1/V2/V3 = 5.29/7.43/6.63; post-test 6.57/8.43/7.60.
- The quoted sentence appears verbatim in the PDF.
- The Kruskal-Wallis statistics reproduce exactly from the raw data: V1 vs V2 chi2(1)=5.5844, p=0.01812; V1 vs V3 chi2(1)=1.81, p=0.1785.
- Text: "the learners with variants 2 and 3 achieved significantly better results than the control group".
- The abstract does say "Segmented videos resulted in higher learning gains than the non-segmented version", so the critique is fair.
- Reading-note arithmetic holds: diff/segmented score = 22.1%, 13.6% (the paper truncates to 13), 28.8%; diff/control = 28.3%, 15.7%, 40.5%.

No contradiction found. WebSearch was unavailable (200/200 budget used), so the contradicting-evidence check was this raw-data re-analysis plus Crossref, which lists no correction or retraction.

Qualifications. These do not falsify the claim, but "supported more than separate shorter videos" must not be read as V2 > V3:
1. V2 vs V3 on gain is not significant: KW chi2(1)=0.42, p=0.52; Welch p=0.37; mean difference 0.80. The authors' R script runs this test but the paper omits it. The paper's own H3 concludes parity ("Thus, H3 can be confirmed").
2. The omnibus 3-group test is not significant (ANOVA F(2,19)=2.945, p=0.0769, which the author notes in his script; KW p=0.080). It is unreported, with no multiplicity correction.
3. The paper's "significantly better" post-test for V3 has no test behind it and does not reproduce (V1 vs V3 KW p=0.27; V1 vs V2 p=0.031). V3's post-test mean is 7.625, not 7.60.
4. Internal inconsistencies:
   - The H3 sentence gives V2 M=7.25, SD=1.16 (Table 6: 7.43, 1.13), so its "9.4%" would be 12.1% with the table value.
   - Group 2 is given as 7, 8 and 10 people in different places.
   - The paper's second "22%" (V3 gain) is 20.2% or 25.3% under either convention.
5. Attrition is differential: 9->7, 12->7 and 17->8 across arms (78%, 58%, 47% retained). Other limits: identical pre- and post-test items, a convenience sample of CS students and colleagues, and an immediate test only.
votes.counterSource: Qualifying, not refuting. Paper PDF https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10758-024-09745-2.pdf (Sect. 3.2 H3 sentence; Tables 4 and 6). Crossref record 10.1007/s10758-024-09745-2 (no correction).

votes.evidence:
NOT REFUTED. Every checkable statement matches the primary source, and I reproduced the statistics from the authors' open data.

1) Primary text. I read the CC-BY version-of-record PDF (Seidel, Technology, Knowledge and Learning 29:1965-1991, published 5 Jul 2024, doi 10.1007/s10758-024-09745-2). Crossref lists no erratum or update. Study 2 text and tables:
- Participants were "randomly assigned to a video type ... and segmentation variant". 22 of the 38 who started were analysed (57.8 %).
- The lecture runs "1 hr 6 min 28 s" and the documentary 50 min 18 s. The tests are 10 multiple-choice items.
- Table 6 "All" rows give mean gain / post-test: variant 1 = 5.29 / 6.57, variant 2 = 7.43 / 8.43, variant 3 = 6.63 / 7.60.
- Kruskal-Wallis, variants 1 vs 2: "χ2(1) = 5.5844, p = 0.01812".
- Kruskal-Wallis, variants 1 vs 3: "χ2(1) = 1.81, p = 0.1785 ... not statistically significant".
- Post-test: "variants 2 and 3 achieved significantly better results" (no test reported).
- Abstract: "Segmented videos resulted in higher learning gains than the non-segmented version".

2) Reproduction. The authors' dataset is linked from the paper as OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/28HM4, which points to GitHub CATALPAresearch/TKNL-YouTube-Video-Length-And-Video-Segmentation, file data-segmentation.csv. Filtering on complete==1 gives n = 7/7/8. Mean gains are 5.286, 7.429 and 6.625. Kruskal-Wallis 1v2 gives χ²=5.5844, p=0.0181, and 1v3 gives χ²=1.8100, p=0.1785. Both match the paper exactly. The reading-note arithmetic also holds:
- Relative to the segmented variant: 1.86/8.43 = 22.1 %, 1.03/7.60 = 13.5 %, 2.14/7.43 = 28.8 %.
- Relative to control: 28.3 %, 15.7 % and 40.5 %.

3) Caveats the claim should travel with. None falsifies it.
- "Supported more" is only about p-values against control. The v2-vs-v3 contrast, which the paper never tests, is χ²(1)=0.42, p=0.52 (mean difference 0.80, bootstrap 95% CI -0.75 to 2.43). That gives no ranking of the two designs. The paper's own H3 line ("variant 2 ... 9.4 % better") is untested.
- The omnibus 3-arm Kruskal-Wallis is χ²(2)=5.06, p=0.080 (the author's R script notes an ANOVA p of 0.0769). Holm-adjusted p for 1v2 over three pairwise tests is 0.054.
- Attrition: starters per arm were 9/12/17, analysed 7/7/8.
- The paper's post-test "significant" for variant 3 has no test behind it (my Kruskal-Wallis p≈0.27). Its 7.60 is really 7.625 in the data.
- The four exclusions include a documentary participant with 19 % watch time, contradicting the paper's "<10 %, all lecture" statement. Adding that participant back gives variant 2 M=7.25 (the figure in the paper's H3 paragraph) and 1v2 p=0.020, so the headline survives.
- The paper's second "22 %" (variant 3 gain) does not fit the formula (20.2 %).
- Participants were mostly computer-science students and colleagues, with an immediate post-test only. Transfer to Class 10/12 revision videos is weak.

I could not refute the claim; every figure in it matches the primary source and the authors' open data. WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted), so I checked directly instead.

What I checked
- Full text of Seidel, "Short, Long, and Segmented Learning Videos", Technology, Knowledge and Learning 29:1965-1991, published 5 July 2024. It is open access under CC BY 4.0, with Niels Seidel as sole author. I read Section 3 and Tables 4 to 6 in a browser, because curl and WebFetch were stopped by Springer's client-challenge page, which I did not try to bypass.
- The authors' public dataset, OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/28HM4, which links to the GitHub repo CATALPAresearch/TKNL-YouTube-Video-Length-And-Video-Segmentation (file data-segmentation.csv, a 2.4 KB CSV fetched read-only). I re-ran the tests myself.

Every claim element matches the paper
- N=22: "22 of the 38 persons who had started" (57.8 %), 14 male and 8 female. Table 4 gives n=7, 7 and 8 for variants 1, 2 and 3.
- Participants were "randomly assigned to a video type (lecture or documentary) and segmentation variant".
- The lecture is "duration 1 hr 6 min 28 s" (= 66 min 28 s) and the documentary "duration 50 min 18 s". The pre-test and post-test are 10 multiple-choice questions.
- Variant 1 vs variant 2: "chi2(1) = 5.5844, p = 0.01812 ... variant 2 (7.43) is higher than that of variant 1 (5.29)". This matches the supporting quote.
- Variant 1 vs variant 3: "chi2(1) = 1.81, p = 0.1785 ... variant 1 (5.29) and variant 3 (6.63) are not statistically significant".
- Post-test: the paper says variants 2 and 3 "achieved significantly better results than the control group", with M=8.43 and 7.60 against 6.57, but reports no test for it. The claim's wording "reported as significantly better" is accurate.
- The abstract says "Segmented videos resulted in higher learning gains than the non-segmented version of the same video", which is indeed stronger than the variant-3 result. The discussion itself concedes "not significantly and less than in the comparison of variants 1 and 2".
- The percentage note is arithmetically right. The paper's "a good 22 %", "13 %" and "almost 29 %" equal 1.86/8.43 = 22.1 %, 1.03/7.60 = 13.6 % and 2.14/7.43 = 28.8 %, so they use the segmented variant as denominator. Relative to control they are 28.3 %, 15.7 % and 40.5 %. These round to the claim's 28 %, 16 % and 40 %.

Independent re-analysis of the authors' data (complete==1, n=22)
- Kruskal-Wallis on learning gain, variant 1 vs 2: chi2(1)=5.5844, p=0.01812. This reproduces the paper exactly.
- Variant 1 vs 3: chi2(1)=1.8100, p=0.17851. Also exact.
- Learning-gain means are 5.286, 7.429 and 6.625.

Qualifiers I found (none changes what the claim literally says)
- The claim's inference that chapters inside one video are "supported more" than separate videos rests on a significant versus non-significant contrast. Variant 2 vs 3 on learning gain is not significant (chi2(1)=0.42, p=0.52). The three-group omnibus test is also not significant (chi2(2)=5.06, p=0.080). The paper never runs the variant 2 vs 3 test.
- On post-test scores my Kruskal-Wallis gives variant 1 vs 2 p=0.031 but variant 1 vs 3 p=0.27. The paper's "significantly better" for variant 3 is therefore not supported by its own data. The claim hedges this correctly with "reported as".
- The paper has small internal inconsistencies:
  - The variant 3 post-test mean is 7.60 in the paper but 7.625 in the raw data.
  - The H3 paragraph gives variant 2's gain as 7.25 (SD 1.16), against 7.43 (SD 1.13) in Table 6.
  - The text says group 2 had 8 or 10 people, but Table 4 says 7.
  - The design section says about 45 min of video, but the videos are 50 and 66 min.
  - The paper's "22 %" for variant 3's learning gain fits neither method: 1.34/6.63 = 20.2 %, or 25.3 % relative to control.
- Threats to validity: 16 of 38 starters (42 %) dropped out, and completion differed by arm (variant 1 7/9, variant 2 7/12, variant 3 8/17). The sample was convenience-based adults (computer-science students and colleagues, 17 aged 25-45). There was an immediate post-test only and no multiple-comparison correction. The result is tentative single-study evidence and says nothing about school students or 15-minute videos.

Source quality and currency
- The source is a peer-reviewed primary paper with open data. It is current (July 2024; today is 2026-10-08).
- There is no correction or retraction: Crossref update-to and updated-by are null, and the Springer page carries no notice.
- None of the 25 works that Semantic Scholar lists as citing it is a replication or critique.

claim: The Study 2 evidence comes from a small sample unlike ExamLeaf's audience. Of 38 people who started, 22 were analysed (14 male, 8 female; 17 aged 25-45, 2 under 25, 3 over 45), recruited by e-mail among computer science students and colleagues. Learning was measured only immediately after viewing, and the author says long-term effects need follow-up tests. No school-age learners or exam-preparation setting are reported. The 4 people who quit early and the 4 excluded for watching under 10 % were all in the lecture-video (66 min) group, which the paper does not analyse as a length effect; lecture and documentary also differ in genre.
quote: Computer science students and colleagues were invited to participate in the study by e-mail.

claim: Seidel's Study 1 covered German and English YouTube Education channels (895 German channels with 83,558 videos; 524 sampled English channels with 154,370 videos). Two-thirds of videos were shorter than about 14 min (DE) and about 23 min (EN); the abstract says 22 for English, a small internal discrepancy. Mean lengths were 14.63 min (DE) and 15.07 min (EN). About 8 % of short and 21 % (DE) / 14 % (EN) of medium-length videos belonged to a segmented series. He notes that researchers' definitions of 'short' (4 min on YouTube; under 6 min for MOOCs per Guo et al. 2014, except tutorials) are far below this practice. This describes what creators do, not what works best, and topic, production style and target audience (e.g. K12) were not examined in detail.
quote: shorter than about 14 min (DE) and about 23 min (EN)

claim: Seidel cites a meta-analysis by Mayer and Pilegard (2014) as showing a segmentation effect in 10 of 10 studies with a median effect size of 0.79. He cites Brame (2016) and Risko et al. (2013) for the view that short videos are meant to prevent passivity and mind-wandering. Both are second-hand literature claims reported in his introduction and background, not results of his own studies, and the originals were not checked here.
quote: a segmentation effect in 10 out of 10 studies examined

"MAINLY LONG, NOT ~15 MIN" HOLDS

CAVEATS THAT DO NOT BREAK THE CLAIM
1. The quote is only a title fragment. The primary source itself supports every number.
2. "Incumbent" is loose. This channel is under 7 months old, and older Assam-medium channels are bigger and use short chapter videos. On 180-video samples:
   - Gyanam Tuition has 142K subscribers (joined 2020) and a median of about 19 min.
   - Pythagoras Classes has 54.2K subscribers (joined 2022) and a median of about 14 min.
   Do not generalise the finding to the Assam market.

The phrase does appear in 15 of PW Bangla's top-60 titles (e.g. "দ্রবণ (Solutions) | Full Chapter in 1 Video | Pure Bangla | Class 12"), so it was lifted from another channel. It is a title fragment and supports none of the statistics.

2) WHAT REPRODUCES (Videos tab only). 
- PW Bangla: subscribers 6.01 lakh; top-30 median 123.2 min; 27 of 30 over 60 min; nine lectures at 315K-429K views. 
- Let's Approach: 2.09 lakh subscribers; 20 of its top 30 over 60 min; six Q&A videos of 1:43:07 to 3:11:10 at 138K-274K views.

votes.evidence:
I rechecked directly on YouTube's public channel pages on 8 Oct 2026. WebSearch was unavailable (budget exhausted).

1) The Videos-tab numbers are accurate, so nothing was fabricated. PW Bangla top-30: 27 videos over 60 min, median 123.2 min, nine lectures at 429K to 315K. Let's Approach: 20 over 60 min, six chapter Q&As of 1:43:07 to 3:11:10 at 138K to 274K. Som's Classroom: shortest 30.1 min, median 54.2. Latest-30 medians: 7.5 min (21 at or under 10 min), 15.8 min (24K median views) and 24.9 min.

2) The cited source and quote do not support it. @PWAssam-Science is "PW Assam HS Science" (15.8K subscribers, joined 17 Mar 2026), none of the three channels analysed. "Full Chapter in 1 Video" appears in none of its 106 video titles, 151 stream titles or 9 playlist titles. It does appear in 7 of PW Bangla's top-30 titles. The cited channel's own top-30 shows the opposite pattern: median 6.7 min, 25 of 30 at or under 10 min, only one video over 60 min, 2.5K to 12K views.

3) The headline inference, a split between long all-time hits and short "current output", is contradicted by the same channels' Live (Streams) tabs. Past live classes are filed there, not under Videos, so "latest 30 uploads" leaves out the long-form output. Last 4 weeks, fully paged:
- PW Bangla: 41 uploads (median 7.6 min, 5.4 h, 0.59M views) versus 58 live streams (median 160 min, 198 h, 2.9M views; median views 35.5K versus 11K).
- Som's Classroom: 27 uploads (median 15.7 min, 6.5 h) versus 27 streams (median 230 min, 138 h; median views 55K versus 24K).
- Let's Approach: 16 uploads (median 26 min) versus 31 streams (median 69 min).
- Items over 60 min were 53%, 44% and 47% of items, 95%, 94% and 70% of content hours, and 76%, 73% and 44% of views.
- Streams-tab all-time top-30 medians are 178, 405 and 66 min.
- Recent long streams already match the "all-time hit" levels. Som's has five streams of 3h18m to 10h39m at 164K to 231K views, against a Videos-tab top-30 floor of 136K. PW Bangla's 8h18m Bengali marathon has 175K against a 170K floor.
So age is not the main confound. Where YouTube files the content is, and current output is still mostly long-form. That misleads on a short-versus-long video decision.

4) Smaller overstatements:
- "1-4 h chapter lectures" conflicts with Som's median of 54 min, with 19 of its top 30 at an hour or less.
- PW Bangla's #1 video (772K) is a 15:41 launch promo, and 3 of its top 30 are under 20 min.
- Ages run from under 1 to 8 years, not 2 to 6. Three Let's Approach top-30 one-shots of 2h49m to 5h09m are only 8 to 11 months old.

Re-source to the three channels and add the Live-tab data before using any of this.
